items.title: Generation of large-amplitude squeezed cat states with near-unity efficiency
items.authors: Simon K. Yung, Matthew S. Winnel, Timothy C. Ralph, Jie Zhao
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Repeated QND-based measurement-induced cat amplification prepares large-amplitude cat states without post-selection on specific photon numbers; success probability reaches 80.64% after 6 rounds for GKP-breeding resources yielding at least 10 dB effective squeezing, scaling with target fidelity F ≈1 - 0.03/n_tot for n_tot ≥3.
items.question: How can optical large-amplitude squeezed cat states suitable for Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill breeding protocols be generated with near-deterministic efficiency?
items.prior: Single-round 6 dB squeezer cat preparation achieves a success probability of 0.16% for n_tot ≥8.
items.limits: Requires photon-number resolving detection and inline optical squeezing; susceptible to optical loss per squeezer and detector inefficiency.
items.tools: quantum non-demolition (QND) interactions · photon-number resolving (PNR) detectors · inline optical squeezing · feedforward Gaussian displacement
items.caption: Schematic of the iterative cat amplification protocol and Wigner distributions across successive rounds, demonstrating increasing cat amplitude and breeding into approximate GKP states.
items.abstract: The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill encoding has emerged as a leading candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computation with continuous variables. For photonic architectures, the major challenge is preparing high-quality resource states, which can be deterministically synthesised from many large-amplitude cat states. Thus far, only modest-sized optical cat states have been prepared experimentally, and the implemented methods are highly probabilistic. We propose an all-optical scheme utilising quantum non-demolition interactions and photon-number measurements to prepare large-amplitude cat states with near-unity probability. Importantly, no particular photon-number outcome is postselected: all outcomes contribute to the accumulated photon number, with the protocol repeated until a required threshold is reached. We demonstrate that the scheme is robust to realistic levels of photon-loss, the dominant source of error in optical systems. Our results highlight the power of active Gaussian operations for state preparation and pave the way for efficient quantum error correction using bosonic codes.

items.title: Phase-sensitive avalanche quantum sensing of sub-shot-noise fields
items.authors: Nikolai D. Klimkin, Misha Ivanov
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Trapped atomic cloud in cavity tuned to a parity-forbidden second-harmonic mode amplifies sub-shot-noise coherent displacement |α_p|²=0.5 by over two orders of magnitude into macroscopic emission while preserving input optical phase.
items.question: Can avalanche amplification detect sub-shot-noise quantum light fluctuations without destroying phase information?
items.limits: Numerical simulation of N_e=60 two-level atoms; classical driver flat-top envelope with peak Rabi frequency 0.1ω₀ and CEP-averaged; ignores thermal bath and inter-atomic collisions.
items.tools: Hierarchy of Pure States (HOPS) method · Tight-binding cavity waveguide model · Two-level atom ensemble model · Multimode Husimi function analysis
items.caption: Normalized output field ⟨hatF ⟩/ √⟨hatF² ⟩_vac versus time for input perturbation phases π/2, π, 3π/2, and 2π. Macroscopic emission rises well above shot noise while preserving the input π/2 phase increments.
items.abstract: Avalanche-based detection of small perturbations is commonplace in precision measurement devices from Geiger counters to single-photon avalanche detectors. Here, we expand this principle to sensing of light waves below the quantum shot noise limit, demonstrating numerically how atomic clouds trapped in photonic cavities can exhibit non-perturbative sensitivity to changes in the cavity field when the cavity mode is tuned to a parity-prohibited transition. We find that, when pumped by a continuous-wave laser, the atomic cloud creates emissions which amplify the initially sub-shot-noise fluctuation by two orders of magnitude. Crucially, this amplification is broadly tunable with respect to frequency and independent of atomic energy structure. Even more strikingly, our amplification mechanism preserves the phase imparted on the atoms by the original ultra-weak light wave, marking a qualitative improvement over conventional protocols. Our finding has implications for both quantum state characterization and detection of weak classical signals.

items.title: All-Microwave Multiqubit Gates
items.authors: Guanqi Wang, Yao Song, Peng-Bo Li, Xiu-Hao Deng
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Single-step (n+m) multiqubit gates implemented on transmon networks via cross-resonance drives without tunable couplers. Three-qubit gates reach simulated fidelities >99.9% in 60ns.
items.question: How can single-step multiqubit gates with n control and m target transmons be implemented with all-microwave control without tunable couplers?
items.limits: Numerical simulation only. Dispersive regime with shared or near-degenerate target frequencies and suppressed parasitic terms such as ZXX.
items.tools: cross-resonance microwave drives · quad frame rotation · block diagonalization · gradient-based pulse optimization
items.caption: Gate infidelity versus optimization iteration and target Pauli operation fidelity across three-qubit gates and larger multi-target configurations, showing convergence below 10⁻³.
items.abstract: Implementing high-fidelity multiqubit gates is critical for reducing circuit depth in near-term quantum processors and fault-tolerant architectures. However, realizing multiqubit interactions and entanglement remains a critical challenge that limits the implementation of multiqubit gates. Here we propose an all-microwave scheme to realize single-step multiqubit gates incorporating n control and m target qubits, tailored for frequency-tunable superconducting transmon networks. By leveraging cross-resonance (CR) drives, this approach induces effective two-body ZX interactions that are significantly stronger than those achieved in conventional resonant regimes, circumventing the need for tunable couplers. The system's effective Hamiltonian is analytically derived using both quad frame rotation and rigorous block diagonalization. These combined theoretical methods facilitate the identification of optimal parameter regimes that simultaneously enhance desired target couplings and suppress parasitic higher-order terms, such as ZXX interactions. Through numerical simulations and gradient-based pulse-shape optimization, we demonstrate three-qubit gates achieving fidelities exceeding 99.9% within a 60 ns gate duration. Furthermore, we evaluate the fundamental scalability of this framework by extending the optimization to a five-qubit CXXXX architecture, confirming the physical viability of the multi-target driving scheme. Because these multiqubit operations naturally emulate stabilizer measurements, this architecture provides a hardware-efficient strategy for reducing the circuit depth of stabilizer-type operations by replacing sequential two-qubit gate decompositions with single-step multiqubit gates.

items.title: Parallel algebraic surgery for qLDPC codes with constant shuttling depth
items.authors: Tian-Gang Zhou, Boren Gu, Jens Eisert, Chen Zhao
items.matched: Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits
items.result: Constructs algebraic surgery directly over group algebras of cyclic lifted-product codes, yielding constant shuttling depth O(1) on 2D neutral-atom arrays. A syndrome cycle with 33 parallel logical measurements is roughly 2× faster than single-observable graph-based surgery schedules.
items.question: Can the parallelism and reconfigurable connectivity of neutral-atom processors implement high-rate quantum LDPC logical operations without prohibitive shuttling overhead?
items.prior: Graph-based surgery auxiliary constructions require general ancilla matchings with O(logw) shuttling depth on atom arrays and roughly double the memory cycle time.
items.limits: Restricted to parallel measurements satisfying cyclic-symmetry or cyclically invariant subspace constraints; evaluated via numerical shuttling-time models and phenomenological/circuit noise simulations without experimental execution.
items.tools: Lifted-product (LP) codes over F₂[x]/(x^l+1) · Acousto-optic deflector (AOD) shuttling · Stim circuit simulations · Relay-BP and BP-LSD decoders · QDistRnd distance estimator
items.caption: Syndrome-extraction cycle times (broken into shuttling and gate times) and total qubit counts across lifted-product code instances (l=9, 15, 33), comparing memory, algebraic surgery, and graph-based surgery schedules.
items.abstract: Reconfigurable atom arrays provide a promising platform for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes, but their computational advantage depends on whether logical operations can be implemented without incurring prohibitive shuttling and space overheads. We introduce algebraic surgery for lifted product codes, co-designing the logical measurements, auxiliary codes, and atom shuttling to enable hardware-efficient Pauli-product measurements. These protocols provide flexible logical addressability subject to the cyclic-symmetry constraint, enabling a broad class of parallel logical measurements, including canonical logical operators with heavily overlapping physical supports and joint measurements within or between code blocks even with different lift sizes, while achieving constant shuttling depth on neutral-atom processors under explicit layout assumptions. In a representative hardware-model benchmark, a cycle supporting 33 parallel canonical logical measurements is about 2× faster than the compared single-observable graph-based surgery schedules, with competitive qubit overhead. These shuttling and circuit-level simulations confirm that the algebraic structure of quantum low-density parity-check codes can be used not only to reduce space overhead, but also to simplify physical implementation and expand the set of efficiently accessible logical operations on neutral-atom processors.

items.title: CSS codes for Quantum Metrology with Discrete-time Error Correction
items.authors: Ugnė Liaubaitė, Debora Ramacciotti, Robert Raußendorf
items.matched: photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling
items.result: Discrete-time CSS quantum error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling δω∝T⁻¹ against perpendicular noise within an interrogation window scaling as t_p ∼1/τ, before crossing over to SQL-like scaling δω∝T^(-1/2). Single recovery applied solely at interrogation end yields zero metrological advantage.
items.question: How does finite-frequency discrete error correction with Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes preserve parameter sensitivity and affect the Heisenberg-to-SQL crossover under perpendicular Markovian noise?
items.limits: Instantaneous and ideal recovery operations; initial logical-plus state |+_L⟩^(⊗k) without noise optimization; local Z signal Hamiltonian and perpendicular Markovian X noise.
items.tools: CSS stabilizer codes (Steane, Shor) · Adjoint Lindblad master equation · Discrete syndrome extraction and recovery map · Classical Fisher information of stabilizer projector
items.caption: Frequency sensitivity versus total sensing time budget T for Steane and Shor codes across correction intervals τ. Sensitivity scales linearly (T⁻¹) up to optimal interrogation time t_opt, then transitions to square-root scaling (T^(-1/2)).
items.abstract: The goal of quantum metrology is to estimate an unknown parameter with better-than-classical precision and, ideally, to attain Heisenberg scaling. In realistic settings, however, noise can substantially reduce this advantage and, in many cases, restore standard-quantum-limit-like performance. Preserving the quantum enhancement therefore requires noise-robust strategies, which can be implemented using quantum error correction. In this work, we develop and analyze a quantum-metrology protocol based on Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. The main result is that, for noise perpendicular to the sensing Hamiltonian, discrete-time error correction preserves Heisenberg-like temporal scaling over a finite interrogation-time window whose duration depends on the correction frequency. It is further shown that recovery applied only after the sensing evolution provides no metrological advantage over the corresponding uncorrected noisy protocol in the setup considered here. An analytical framework is developed for arbitrary CSS codes and applied to the Steane and Shor codes, for which the discrete-time corrected dynamics, the Heisenberg-like-to-SQL-like crossover, and the optimal interrogation time are determined and numerically analysed.

items.title: Proposal for matter-wave interferometry with a rare-earth-doped microparticle
items.authors: Chris Overstreet
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Proposed Mach-Zehnder matter-wave interferometer for a rare-earth-doped microparticle reaches up to 10³ photons per beam splitter with millisecond coherence time. Mass-scaling keeps external decoherence rates constant or decreasing in the long-wavelength limit λ≫Δx.
items.question: How can matter-wave interference be observed for a microparticle without requiring ground-state cooling, orientational control, or ultrahigh vacuum?
items.prior: Gravitationally mediated entanglement requires mass ∼10¹² amu, a factor of 10⁷ higher than existing matter-wave interferometry.
items.limits: Cryogenic environment ( ≈6 K) and moderate vacuum (10⁻⁶ Torr); microparticle material requires maximum phonon frequency lesssim7 THz.
items.tools: Mach-Zehnder geometry · two-photon Raman transitions · ⁶F_(1/2) state of Sm³⁺ in SrSe · Judd-Ofelt theory · buffer-gas cooling
items.caption: Calculated background gas decoherence rate as a function of microparticle mass for 2ℏk and 1000ℏk momentum transfers at 10⁻⁶ Torr and 6 K.
items.abstract: Matter-wave interferometers are sensitive probes of low energy physics and have been used for precise tests of gravity and quantum mechanics. These applications would benefit from interfering particles of higher mass, but observing the interference of a large particle is challenging due to the need to control its initial state and to avoid decoherence. Here we propose to demonstrate matter-wave interference of a microparticle with an embedded rare-earth ion. Optical transitions of the rare-earth ion will impart momentum to the microparticle's center of mass. The use of a time-symmetric interferometer geometry and a rare-earth ion state with angular momentum J = 1/2 will eliminate sensitivity to the initial conditions of the microparticle. We show that the rates of all relevant external decoherence mechanisms either decrease or remain constant as the microparticle mass is increased, allowing decoherence to be avoided by using sufficiently large particles. An apparatus at moderate vacuum levels will support microparticle interferometry with up to 10³ photons per beam splitter and millisecond coherence time. This demonstration will establish microparticle interferometry as a new platform for quantum sensing, improving searches for minimal modifications of quantum mechanics by up to four orders of magnitude in the near term and laying the foundation for future gravitational tests.

items.title: Quantum double lock-in detection via sequential orthogonal quantum mixing
items.authors: Min Zhuang, Sijie Chen, Jiahao Huang, Chaohong Lee
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Single-interferometer quantum double lock-in detection extracts amplitude A, frequency ω, and initial phase β of an oscillating signal, achieving Heisenberg-limited precisions ΔA, Δω, Δβ∝1/N with an N-particle GHZ probe and interaction-based readout.
items.question: Can quantum double lock-in detection extract full amplitude, frequency, and phase information from an unknown oscillating signal using a single quantum interferometry while achieving Heisenberg-limited precision?
items.prior: Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two separate quantum interferometers, each requiring state preparation and readout (was ∝1/√N scaling without entanglement).
items.limits: Theoretical derivation assuming instantaneous π pulses and noiseless state initialization. Gaussian detection noise σ= 0.5√N degrades scaling to between SQL and Heisenberg limit.
items.tools: Periodic dynamical decoupling (PDD) sequences · Carr-Purcell (CP) sequences · Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states · Fast Fourier transform (FFT) / Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) analysis
items.caption: Log-log scaling of measurement precisions ΔA, Δω, and Δβ versus particle number N, showing 1/√N standard quantum limit for spin-coherent states and 1/N Heisenberg scaling for GHZ states.
items.abstract: High-precision measurement of oscillating signal is a ubiquitous issue in fundamental science and a critical task in practical technologies. In quantum metrology, quantum lock-in detection provide an efficient method for measuring such signal. In general, when the initial phase of the oscillating signal is unknown,quantum double lock-in detection can effectively extract complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two individual quantum interferometry, each of which must undergo state preparation and readout. However, the time for state preparation and readout need not be negligible in practical experiments. In particular, the time for state preparation is longer than the time for sensing. To save experimental resources, it is challenging to achieve quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry while still extracting complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Here, we present a general protocol for achieving a quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry under a sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences. In particular, if the input state is a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and two interaction-based operations are applied during interferometry, the measurement precisions for frequency, amplitude, and initial phase can both approach the Heisenberg limit. Our study paves a new way for measuring oscillating signals with a single quantum interferometry, and provides a feasible method for achieving Heisenberg-limited detection of alternating signals.

items.title: Entangling Atomic Quantum Memories Using High-Order Modulated Coherent States
items.authors: Chaohan Cui, Prajit Dhara, Saikat Guha
items.matched: Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons
items.result: Square-root-measurement-inspired 16-QAM receiver achieves 1.75 ebits per mode at 0.5 dB end-to-end loss, 3.8 dB below the two-way assisted single-half-link PLOB capacity. Variational 32-outcome POVM increases 4-QAM rate by 4.0% over the square-root measurement to 1.1289 ebits per mode.
items.question: Can high-order coherent-state modulation distribute multiple ebits per optical mode between stationary atomic memories through a collective midpoint measurement?
items.prior: was at most 0.46 ebits per mode at 0.5 dB end-to-end loss for single-photon baseline links
items.limits: Pure-loss channels; advantage over single-photon protocols requires per-interface loss lesssim0.2 dB and systematic phase error |δφ|lesssim0.2π; physical linear-optical implementation of the collective midpoint POVM remains open.
items.tools: square-root measurement (SRM) POVM · reflective cavity qubit-photon interfaces · M-QAM coherent-state modulation · two-way coherent information (hashing bound) · variational POVM optimization
items.caption: Entanglement distribution rate per mode versus end-to-end channel loss L_ch (dB) for various M-QAM orders compared to single-photon baselines and the PLOB capacity limit.
items.abstract: High-order coherent-state modulation with reflective cavity-coupled atomic memories can distribute multiple heralded ebits per transmitted optical mode, but requires a collective midpoint POVM optimized for maximum distillable entanglement rather than minimum-error state discrimination. An SRM-inspired 16-QAM receiver reaches 1.75 ebits per mode at 0.5~dB end-to-end loss, 3.8~dB below the half-link capacity benchmark. For 4-QAM, a variational POVM with more outcomes than constellation points improves the SRM rate by 4.0% yet remains below capacity, revealing measurement-design headroom. The advantage over single-qubit-per-mode midpoint protocols persists for per-interface loss <0.2~dB and calibrated phase error <0.2π.

items.title: Constant-Overhead Injection into Quantum Codes
items.authors: Louis Golowich, Venkatesan Guruswami
items.matched: quantum LDPC codes and low-overhead fault tolerance
items.result: Fault-tolerant injection and ejection between bare physical qubits and [[n = Θ(k), k, d = poly(k)]] quantum error-correcting codes achieves O(k) space and O(1) quantum circuit depth under locally stochastic circuit noise.
items.question: Can state injection and ejection between bare physical qubits and quantum error-correcting codes be performed fault-tolerantly with constant space and time overhead?
items.limits: Requires polynomial-sized noiseless classical computation per timestep; errors on bare physical qubits are not fully independent across all sites.
items.tools: hypergraph product codes · Spielman linear-time classical LDPC codes · small-set flip decoding · code concatenation with non-uniform block sizes
items.caption: A protocol for switching between quantum code states Q₁ and Q'₁ by injecting physical qubits into an intermediate code Q₂, executing the encoding transformation fault-tolerantly, and ejecting.
items.abstract: We construct the first known fault-tolerant scheme for injecting states into quantum error-correcting codes with constant space and time overhead. That is, we construct a family of constant-rate quantum error-correcting codes for which a set of bare physical qubits can be injected, i.e. fault-tolerantly encoded, into a code block. Similarly, a code state can be ejected, i.e. fault-tolerantly decoded, back into bare physical qubits. We show that these injection and ejection procedures succeed under circuit-level locally stochastic noise, while incurring just a small constant probability of corrupting each qubit, which is unavoidable for bare physical qubits. We also show how to perform fault-tolerant error correction and code-state preparation under locally stochastic noise. All of our gadgets can be implemented with constant quantum circuit depth (i.e. are single-shot), and with a number of physical qubits growing linearly with the number of logical qubits, assuming the ability to run polynomial-sized noiseless classical circuits on the side. We construct our quantum codes by taking a high-dimensional hypergraph product of classical LDPC codes, which in turn are a simplified version of Spielman's linear-time encodable codes (STOC'95). As our resulting product codes are only resilient to physical errors occurring with non-uniform probabilities across qubits, we then show how to concatenate with inner codes of various sizes to obtain fault-tolerance against uniform noise.

items.title: Theory of spacetime quantum fault tolerance
items.authors: Yijia Xu, Yixu Wang, Zi-Wen Liu
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Formulated unified algebraic framework for Clifford spacetime fault tolerance using spacetime chain complexes constructed from tensor networks, capturing gauge/stabilizer structures, fault propagation, and logical operations.
items.question: Can spacetime codes, gadget-level fault tolerance, and various noise models be unified into a single algebraic formalism?
items.limits: Restricted to Clifford spacetime circuits and Pauli fault models.
items.tools: spacetime chain complexes · tensor network representations · Clifford circuit gauge/stabilizer structures · homological algebra
items.abstract: We present a unified algebraic theory of Clifford spacetime quantum fault tolerance, which underpins universal fault-tolerant quantum computation. We construct a spacetime chain complex from a tensor network representation of a circuit that encodes fault propagation, detector syndromes, and logical actions through the associated gauge and stabilizer structure. We show that this theory (1) unifies various formulations of quantum fault tolerance including spacetime codes, Gottesman's gadget framework, fault complexes, and ZX calculus; (2) connects spacetime distances to the gadget-level correctness properties in Gottesman's formalism; (3) naturally accommodates a range of fault models, in particular phenomenological and circuit-level models, bringing these often separately formulated descriptions into a common algebraic framework through different tensor decompositions and fault assignments; and (4) recovers many known fault tolerance constructions and results as special cases, including repeated syndrome extraction, correlated detectors for transversal and fold-transversal gates, Steane- and Knill-type syndrome extraction gadgets, and single-shot error correction.

items.title: Parallel algebraic surgery for qLDPC codes with constant shuttling depth
items.authors: Tian-Gang Zhou, Boren Gu, Jens Eisert, Chen Zhao
items.matched: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
items.result: Constructs algebraic surgery directly over group algebras of cyclic lifted-product codes, yielding constant shuttling depth O(1) on 2D neutral-atom arrays. A syndrome cycle with 33 parallel logical measurements is roughly 2× faster than single-observable graph-based surgery schedules.
items.question: Can the parallelism and reconfigurable connectivity of neutral-atom processors implement high-rate quantum LDPC logical operations without prohibitive shuttling overhead?
items.prior: Graph-based surgery auxiliary constructions require general ancilla matchings with O(logw) shuttling depth on atom arrays and roughly double the memory cycle time.
items.limits: Restricted to parallel measurements satisfying cyclic-symmetry or cyclically invariant subspace constraints; evaluated via numerical shuttling-time models and phenomenological/circuit noise simulations without experimental execution.
items.tools: Lifted-product (LP) codes over F₂[x]/(x^l+1) · Acousto-optic deflector (AOD) shuttling · Stim circuit simulations · Relay-BP and BP-LSD decoders · QDistRnd distance estimator
items.caption: Syndrome-extraction cycle times (broken into shuttling and gate times) and total qubit counts across lifted-product code instances (l=9, 15, 33), comparing memory, algebraic surgery, and graph-based surgery schedules.
items.abstract: Reconfigurable atom arrays provide a promising platform for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes, but their computational advantage depends on whether logical operations can be implemented without incurring prohibitive shuttling and space overheads. We introduce algebraic surgery for lifted product codes, co-designing the logical measurements, auxiliary codes, and atom shuttling to enable hardware-efficient Pauli-product measurements. These protocols provide flexible logical addressability subject to the cyclic-symmetry constraint, enabling a broad class of parallel logical measurements, including canonical logical operators with heavily overlapping physical supports and joint measurements within or between code blocks even with different lift sizes, while achieving constant shuttling depth on neutral-atom processors under explicit layout assumptions. In a representative hardware-model benchmark, a cycle supporting 33 parallel canonical logical measurements is about 2× faster than the compared single-observable graph-based surgery schedules, with competitive qubit overhead. These shuttling and circuit-level simulations confirm that the algebraic structure of quantum low-density parity-check codes can be used not only to reduce space overhead, but also to simplify physical implementation and expand the set of efficiently accessible logical operations on neutral-atom processors.

items.title: Distillation of N-Qubit Stabilizer States on a Star Network Topology
items.authors: Theodore M. Mahaffey, Chaohan Cui, Saikat Guha, Murphy Yuezhen Niu
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Local operations with an [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code distill n copies of an N-qubit GHZ state into k logical copies on a star network, improving output fidelity over a bare transmitted GHZ state for single-qubit depolarizing rates up to 13.8% (5-qubit code) and ≥6% ([[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code).
items.question: How can n copies of an N-qubit multipartite entangled state be distilled into k higher-fidelity logical copies across N network nodes using only local operations and stabilizer codes?
items.prior: Rengaswamy et al. (2021) linear-topology distillation for 3-qubit GHZ states requiring high-weight stabilizer measurements of an intermediate [[2n,k]] code.
items.limits: Independent single-qubit depolarizing noise channel, no measurement errors modeled, noiseless central state factory.
items.tools: stabilizer formalism · star network LOCC distillation protocol · Monte Carlo decoder simulations · bivariate bicycle Gross code · toric code
items.caption: Schematic of the star network entanglement distillation scheme for N=3 and N=4 nodes, distributing n raw copies of an N-qubit GHZ state to yield k logical copies after local code generator measurements.
items.abstract: We introduce an entanglement distillation protocol that utilizes an arbitrary [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code to convert n raw copies of an N-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state into k logical copies in the presence of Pauli noise. Our explicit formulation of the scheme on a star network topology is efficiently scalable to arbitrary N, requires only local operations, and minimizes the impact of errors on idle physical qubits, enabling the distribution of high-fidelity entangled logical states between any number of quantum processors. We report the results of numerical experiments using the 5-qubit code, toric code, and [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicyle code to protect against independent single-qubit depolarizing noise on all qubits. Our encoding scheme improves the final GHZ state fidelity relative to a single bare GHZ state sent over the same noisy channel for depolarizing rates up to or above 6 % for all codes tested. Additionally, we use the stabilizer formalism to prove that our protocol can be applied to any N-qubit Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) stabilizer state, from which the GHZ state emerges as a special case. This result explicitly establishes the working principle of previous stabilizer-based Bell pair and GHZ state distillation schemes, and generalizes such protocols beyond the traditionally considered states. We also show that some stabilizer codes can distill any stabilizer state with our protocol.

items.title: Entropy threshold: A simple proxy for performance of quantum error correction
items.authors: Diego Ruiz, Aleksander Kubica
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Local equality between per-unit-cell noise entropy and syndrome entropy, widetildeH_E(p_⋆)=lim_(i→∞)(m_(i+1)-m_i)/(n_(i+1)-n_i)widetildeH_S(p_⋆), estimates error-correction thresholds across biased Pauli, erasure, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise without Monte Carlo simulations.
items.question: Can quantum error correction thresholds be estimated directly and analytically across diverse codes and noise models without computationally intensive Monte Carlo decoding simulations?
items.prior: was computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations across code sizes and decoders, zero-rate hashing bound (about 11% for depolarizing noise), or statistical-mechanical mappings
items.limits: Requires syndrome bits to be approximately independent near threshold; neglects degeneracy entropy H(E|L,S) (fails for codes with extensive gauge degeneracy such as Bacon-Shor); overly optimistic for soft measurement information.
items.tools: Shannon conditional entropy decomposition · Independent syndrome approximation · Unit-cell entropy rate matching · Tensor network decoding validation
items.caption: Threshold p_th versus noise bias η for surface, XY, and XZZX codes, comparing the local entropy threshold calculation (solid curves) against tensor-network maximum-likelihood decoding (dots). Also shows logical error rate p_L correlated with conditional entropy H(L|S) across all 3^(d²) Clifford deformations at d=3.
items.abstract: The rapidly growing landscape of quantum error-correction (QEC) protocols has produced a wealth of numerical data, but comparatively few heuristics for understanding and predicting their performance. Here, we develop a simple entropy-based proxy that predicts the thresholds of a variety of QEC protocols, ranging from the code-capacity setting of Clifford-deformed surface codes with biased Pauli or erasure noise to the circuit-level noise model of the surface or color codes with flag qubits. Our proxy estimates the threshold by locally comparing the noise entropy with the error information gained via stabilizer measurements (or spacetime detectors and flag outcomes in the circuit-level settings). Despite neglecting correlations between stabilizer outcomes and the contribution from code degeneracy, the proxy captures the main trends across diverse settings and yields threshold estimates in good agreement with numerical results. Our work develops much-needed phenomenology that enables simple back-of-the-envelope estimates of QEC performance, recovering and providing an explanation for the results of computationally intensive detailed simulations.

items.title: Constant Rate Codes with Fully Addressable Transversal T: Good Codes, Sparse Checks
items.authors: Alexander Meiburg
items.matched: Asymptotically good Quantum and locally testable classical LDPC codes
items.result: Explicit asymptotically good CSS codes (k,d = Ω(n)) achieve fully addressable transversal T gate along with transversal logical Paulis. Subsystem construction gives fully addressable transversal T, constant protected rate K=Θ(n), distance Ω(√n), and sparse non-Pauli commuting checks.
items.question: Can quantum error-correcting codes achieve constant rate, macroscopic distance, check sparsity, and logical addressability for transversal non-Clifford gates simultaneously?
items.prior: Wills [5] constructed constant-rate codes with collective transversal T but vanishing rate-distance scaling (subpolynomial distance) and no individual addressability.
items.limits: Asymptotic regime. Sparse protected subsystem code uses non-Pauli commuting checks and leaves a Clifford action on gauge qubits. Pauli-LDPC transversal T variant has k=2 (vanishing rate) and no logical addressability.
items.tools: Garcia-Stichtenoth algebraic geometry towers · Modular clock codes over Z₈ · Hypergraph-product architectures · 28-qubit binary cell embedding · Quaternion quotient of 3D color codes
items.abstract: Recent work by Wills constructed codes with constant rate and transversal T. Extending this line of work, we construct asymptotically good CSS codes with fully addressable transversal T, permitting selective control over which logical qubits receive a T gate. We also give Pauli-LDPC codes with transversal T and growing distance at vanishing rate; and a protected-subsystem construction with fully addressable transversal T, constant protected rate, distance Ω(√n), and sparse (non-Pauli) checks. More generally, we obtain asymptotically good binary codes with full transversal addressability for every fixed finite-order one-qubit gate, retaining CSS realizations for dyadic phase gates such as √T and using generally nonadditive codes for rotations such as R_z(π/7). The remaining challenge is to construct asymptotically good Pauli-LDPC codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford one-qubit gates.

Subsystem construction gives fully addressable transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math>, constant protected rate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mspace></mspace></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mspace></mspace></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mrow><mi>n</mi><mspace width="0pt" height="0.5em"></mspace></mrow></msqrt><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>, and sparse non-Pauli commuting checks.
html.prior: Wills [5] constructed constant-rate codes with collective transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math> but vanishing rate-distance scaling (subpolynomial distance) and no individual addressability.
html.limits: Asymptotic regime. Sparse protected subsystem code uses non-Pauli commuting checks and leaves a Clifford action on gauge qubits. Pauli-LDPC transversal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math> variant has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> (vanishing rate) and no logical addressability.

items.title: The Intrinsic Cost of Quantum Syndrome Extraction
items.authors: Chia-Tung Chu
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Syndrome extraction across a hardware cut L with data U=Q∩L requires at least χ_U/2 crossing quantum operations and χ_U shared Bell pairs, where χ_U=rankH_U+rankH_(U^c)-rankH. For a fixed quantum Tanner code family, exact syndrome extraction on an N-qubit 2D grid achieves the optimal space--depth tradeoff ND_min²=Θ(n²) over n≤N≤cn².
items.question: How much depth does exact syndrome extraction of a stabilizer code require on hardware with a given connectivity graph?
items.prior: Delfosse-Beverland-Tremblay (2021) lower-bounded depth by counting listed check crossings, yielding Ω(n/√N), which is shown to fail for expanding presentations of annular surface codes that actually admit depth-13 extraction.
items.limits: Exact noiseless syndrome extraction, bounded check weight and incidence, classical communication and computation are free, 2D grid hardware.
items.tools: intrinsic cut cost rank formula · relative entropy of entanglement bounds · tiled grid routing compiler · remote parity Bell-pair protocols
items.caption: The grid architecture and 4×4 tile layout used to compile syndrome extraction matchings into O(n/√N) depth via disjoint horizontal/vertical routing paths and local Bell state generation.
items.abstract: How much time is fundamentally required to extract the syndrome of a stabilizer code on hardware with a given connectivity graph? Previous work by Delfosse--Beverland--Tremblay (2021) and Baspin--Fawzi--Shayeghi (2023) established bounds connecting syndrome extraction to locality constraints on quantum hardware. Here, we address this question by first formulating an intrinsic measure of the interaction required for syndrome extraction directly from the stabilizer group, independent of the generating set used to describe the code. We then show that this measure yields hardware-dependent lower bounds on exact syndrome-extraction depth for arbitrary stabilizer codes. Guided by this measure, we also construct annular surface-code examples with constant-depth local syndrome extraction that provide a counterexample to Corollary 1 of DBT21. Furthermore, for a fixed quantum Tanner family, this measure strengthens the depth bound explicitly stated in BFS23 and, together with our matching construction, establishes an asymptotically tight space--depth tradeoff. In theory, our results connect the information required by syndrome extraction to the communication capacity of a device; while in practice, they provide a way to assess unavoidable circuit costs before committing to a hardware layout.

items.title: Layer codes as quantum memories: syndrome extraction, thresholds and idle robustness
items.authors: Zhu Sun, Zhenyu Cai
items.matched: surface code decoders and logical error rates under circuit-level noise
items.result: Layer codes reach a circuit-level threshold of p_th=5.06(7)×10⁻³ in Z memory (4.99(6)×10⁻³ in X) and sustain idle intervals 1.7–3.0 times longer than rotated surface codes at equal distance.
items.question: How do 3D layer codes perform as active quantum memories under noisy syndrome extraction circuits?
items.prior: Rotated surface code threshold was 7.73(14)×10⁻³ in Z (7.71(9)×10⁻³ in X); unrotated was 8.29(6)×10⁻³ in Z (8.02(6)×10⁻³ in X) under the same decoder.
items.limits: Circuit-level depolarizing noise model with per-tick idle. Tested on small CSS input codes ([[4,2,2]], [[6,4,2]], [[7,1,3]], [[9,1,3]]). Requires non-planar cross-plane CNOTs.
items.tools: Hook-constrained constraint-programming scheduler · BP+LSD / BP+OSD decoders on raw DEM · Stim circuit simulations · YBW26 algebraic homology layer code construction
items.caption: Logical error rate per round versus physical error rate for layer codes of distance d=4 to 8, showing the threshold crossing around p ≈5×10⁻³ for X- and Z-basis memories.
items.abstract: Layer codes are three-dimensional local CSS codes of check weight at most six, obtained by quasi-concatenating a CSS input code with unrotated surface code patches. What is established about them describes the code, not the circuit that measures it. In this work, we evaluate them as active memories under circuit-level noise. Doing so first requires a syndrome extraction circuit, and the junction stabilizers that couple the patches rule out borrowing a surface code patch's CNOT schedule. We present a decoder-free scheduler that constrains hook propagation first and compresses depth afterwards, generate circuits for eighteen layer codes across four input codes, and compare them with surface codes of the same distance, simulated and decoded in the same way. The circuits lose no distance to hook errors on [[4,2,2]]-input codes wherever a circuit-distance proof is affordable, and reach a lower logical error rate than those of a general-purpose scheduler for CSS codes at roughly half its CNOT depth per round. Our primary family built from a [[4,2,2]] input code reaches a circuit-level threshold of 5.06(7)×10⁻³. The layer code outperforms the surface code in terms of idle robustness: at the same distance it tolerates an interval between syndrome extraction rounds 1.7-3.0 times longer than the rotated surface code. This comes at the cost of 1.7-5.0 times more operations per unit time and approximately five times more physical qubits, both per logical qubit. Finally, we model the cost of the beyond-2D cross-plane CNOTs that the construction demands, and find that their speed matters far more than their fidelity.

items.title: Resource-Tunable Quantum Circuit Implementation of Nonlinear Element-Wise Transformations
items.authors: Chunlin Yang, Yuqi Li, Hongmei Yao, Zhaobing Fan
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Circuit depth for entry-wise Hadamard matrix polynomial transformations of degree 2^d-1 reduced to O(n+d) via polynomial factorization into m parallel factors, matching the query lower bound of 2^d-1 single-oracle queries when m=2^d-1.
items.question: Can the circuit depth for implementing a Hadamard matrix function on block-encoded data be reduced below linear in the polynomial degree?
items.prior: Linear circuit depth in the polynomial degree with logarithmic auxiliary space (Kao et al. 2024 / Ref. [19]).
items.limits: Entries of input matrix must lie on compact domain Ω⊆C with connected complement CsetminusΩ; relies on post-selection with success probability scaling inversely with the square of the normalization factor α.
items.tools: Polynomial factorization · Block encoding · Quantum Hadamard product (QHP) · Binary-tree recursion
items.caption: Circuit architecture decomposing a Hadamard matrix function into m low-degree factors P^((s))(A) combined via a parallel quantum Hadamard product.
items.abstract: Nonlinear transformations are important in quantum machine learning and other quantum numerical applications, which can be reduced to the implementation of element-wise polynomials through polynomial approximation. Existing works establish the feasibility of transformations and improve query or auxiliary-space efficiency, but circuit depth remains linear in scale with degree. In this work, we develop a resource-tunable quantum framework that decomposes a (2^d-1)-degree polynomial into m lower-degree factors, with m controlling the degree of parallelism. By varying m from 1 to 2^d-1, the framework provides a trade-off among query complexity, additional gate complexity, ancilla count, and normalization, ranging from a binary-tree implementation to a O(n+d)-depth construction with highly parallel oracle queries that match the query lower bound. The effects of polynomial approximation and implementation errors are further analyzed. We demonstrate the framework for nonlinear activation functions such as sigmoid and tanh, as well as pixel-wise image transformations.

items.title: Transducer-based linear combination of unitaries: theory and applications
items.authors: Dong An, Dekuan Dong, Changpeng Shao, Yuxin Zhang, Chenhao Zhao
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Transducer-based linear combination of unitaries implements block-encoding of A/α with rescaling α=O(a) using O(C_maxlog(1/ε) + (λ/a)overlineC(log(1/ε))²) primitive queries. Converts transducer action to ε-approximate block-encoding in O(K log(1/ε)) queries via resolvent norm K.
items.question: Can quantum coherence be preserved in linear combinations of unitaries while reducing query complexity from worst-case to weighted-average cost?
items.prior: Standard LCU with amplitude amplification required widetildeO(C_maxλ/a) queries (Gilyén et al. 2019).
items.limits: Requires constituent unitaries to access a common family of primitive oracles coherently, and requires an a priori upper bound a ≥|A|.
items.tools: transducer framework · resolvent norm analysis · Cayley transformation · finite-reuse catalyst removal · tunable variable-time amplitude amplification
items.abstract: Linear combination of unitaries (LCU) is a fundamental primitive in quantum algorithms, whose cost is typically governed by the most expensive unitary appearing in the combination. We develop a transducer-based LCU framework that reduces this worst-case dependence to a weighted average query complexity, when the constituent unitaries share access to a common set of primitive oracles. Consider A=∑_j c_j U_j, where c_j>0 and each unitary U_j can be implemented using C_j primitive queries. Given an upper bound a≥|A|, our algorithm implements a block-encoding of A/α with rescaling factor α=O(a), using widetildeO (C_max+overlineC λ/a ) primitive queries, where λ=∑_j c_j, C_max=max_j C_j, and overlineC= ∑_j c_j C_j/λ. By comparison, the standard LCU construction requires widetildeO (C_max λ/a ) primitive queries. The improvement can therefore be substantial when costly unitaries have small weights and λ/a is large. As applications, we obtain improved block-encodings of sparse matrices, leading to quantum algorithms for sparse Hamiltonian simulation and quantum linear systems with near-optimal query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors in all relevant parameters. Our main technique is the transducer framework developed by Belovs, Jeffery, and Yolcu [Quantum, 8:1444 (2024)]. Here we develop a complementary operator-level theory tailored to block-encodings. We identify the resolvent norm K as a key complexity measure for transducer implementation besides the existing catalyst complexity. We show that the transducer action can be converted into an ε-approximate block-encoding using only O(K log(1/ε)) queries to the transducer, improving the precision dependence from polynomial to logarithmic.

items.result: Observable estimation ⟨ψ|f(H)^† O_j f(H)|ψ⟩ with QSVT achieves quantum circuit depth O(r D_H) or O(s D_H), where r is the H-invariant Krylov dimension, s ≤r is the observable-visible Krylov dimension, and D_H is the block-encoding depth of H.
items.question: Can we use the QSVT framework to enable end-to-end quantum applications within the coherent circuit depth constraints of early fault-tolerant quantum computers?
items.prior: Standard QSVT circuit depth scales linearly with polynomial degree °(f) independent of state or observable structure.
items.limits: Requires H-invariance or accurate low-dimensional truncation of the Krylov subspace mathscrK_r(H,|ψ⟩), bounded polynomial norm ratios, and well-conditioned Gram/shadow matrices.
items.tools: Krylov subspace methods · Observable-aware quotient spaces · History-state constructions · Classical shadows · Hadamard test
items.abstract: We introduce shadow quantum singular value transformation (Shadow QSVT): given an initial state |ψ⟩, a Hermitian matrix H, a polynomial f, and a set of observables O₁,…,O_m, the goal is to estimate ⟨ψ|f(H)^†O_j f(H)|ψ⟩ for all j∈1,…,m. Shadow QSVT provides a systematic route to reduce the quantum resources required by standard QSVT, which constructs a unitary block-encoding of f(H). It uses structure in the input state and observables, together with the fact that many applications require only observable estimates rather than synthesizing the full unitary. We present three algorithms that exploit structure in the initial state and observables to reduce quantum circuit depth. First, we develop a state-aware QSVT algorithm that prepares the target state with low circuit depth when the Krylov subspace associated with H and |ψ⟩ is low-dimensional or admits an accurate low-dimensional approximation. Second, we introduce an observable-aware Shadow QSVT algorithm that combines a new observable-aware Krylov subspace with history states to further reduce circuit depth and gate complexity. Finally, we develop Classical Shadow QSVT, which constructs a classical representation from H, f, and |ψ⟩ without prior knowledge of the observables or explicit preparation of the target state proportional to f(H)|ψ⟩. This representation enables estimation of the target quantities for observables specified after the quantum computation. Together, these three algorithms provide tools for reducing the circuit depth of QSVT-based computations across a range of settings.

items.title: A physical and universal model of bosonic computations with Solovay-Kitaev theorem
items.authors: Dorian Rudolph, Arsalan Motamedi, Dhruva Sambrani, Hamid Reza Naeij, Ulysse Chabaud, Sevag Gharibian, Saeed Mehraban
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Bosonic Energy-Preserving Quantum Computation (BEQC) model uses energy-conserving gates driven by coherent state ancillae, efficiently simulating polynomial-energy continuous-variable circuits while recovering BQP and enabling Solovay-Kitaev gate compilation.
items.question: How can continuous-variable quantum computation be formulated to prevent unphysical energy blowups and restore universal compilation?
items.prior: Standard Lloyd-Braunstein continuous-variable models allow doubly exponential energy growth in time t, diverging photon numbers, and lack general Solovay-Kitaev compilation guarantees.
items.limits: Simulations of active non-energy-preserving operations require coherent ancilla amplitude α to scale with target precision O(1/ε); computational equivalence to BQP holds specifically in the polynomial-energy regime.
items.tools: Coherent state ancillae · Energy-preserving Hamiltonians · Linear optics and Kerr non-linearities · Lie-Trotter product formulas · Fock space truncation
items.caption: Schematic of the BEQC architecture: vacuum state inputs alongside a coherent-state energy reservoir undergo a sequence of energy-preserving unitaries before final photon-number measurement.
items.abstract: Bosonic quantum systems are among the leading architectures for quantum information processing, offering continuous-variable degrees of freedom with strong error-correction capabilities. However, standard bosonic quantum computation models such as the Lloyd-Braunstein [Lloyd and Braunstein, 1999] and hybrid oscillator-qubit models [Brenner, Dias, and Koenig, 2025; Liu et al., 2026] permit dramatic energy growth, leading to unphysical computational power and the breakdown of fundamental algorithmic tools such as universal and efficient compilation [Brenner et al., 2026; Rudolph et al., 2025]. To address this, we introduce a new model of bosonic quantum computation, Bosonic Energy-Preserving Quantum Computation (BEQC), in which energy is treated as a computational resource. Namely, energy is supplied solely through input coherent states, and all gates are generated by energy-preserving Hamiltonians. Thus, by construction, dramatic energy growth is impossible, making the model physically grounded. We next show that BEQC is a computationally robust and universal model in many respects, including: (1. Computational power) BEQC efficiently simulates all polynomial-energy computations in existing models, and exactly recovers BQP in the polynomial energy setting. It further admits several complexity-theoretic upper bounds when varying the energy, precision, and space parameters of the model. (2. Universal gate sets and state synthesis) BEQC has natural universal gate sets based on linear optics and Kerr interactions. In particular, we obtain a Solovay-Kitaev theorem which circumvents previous no-go results. We give various applications, including (a) a protocol for engineering GKP states with rigorous preparation guarantees, (b) Fock state preparation to exponential precision, and (c) native Fock space simulation of any qubit-based unitary.

items.title: A Quantum Scaling Algorithm for Maximum-Weight Perfect Matching in General Graphs
items.authors: Kourosh Mirsohi, Sandy Irani, Michael T. Goodrich
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Quantum algorithm computes exact maximum-weight perfect matching on general graphs with integer weights up to W in widetildeO(n m^(2/3)logW) time.
items.question: Can quantum algorithms achieve an asymptotic speedup over the best classical combinatorial algorithm for maximum-weight perfect matching on general graphs?
items.prior: Best classical combinatorial bound was widetildeO(m√nlogW) (Duan, Pettie, and Su 2018); this improves it in the dense regime m≥n^(3/2).
items.limits: Asymptotic time bound in the dense regime m≥n^(3/2) under QRAM model with unit-time coherent reads.
items.tools: QRAM model with BBHT Grover search · Primal-dual weight scaling framework · Edmonds blossom contraction and laminar families · Liquidationist matching architecture
items.caption: Schematic of an alternating augmenting path across contracted blossom roots ⟨B₁, …, B_r ⟩, showing original-graph endpoints (u_i, v_i) and matched edges.
items.abstract: Quantum speed-ups have been obtained for many fundamental graph problems, including most variants of matching. A notable exception, however, is the maximum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) problem in general graphs with integer edge weights, which is arguably the most challenging variant of matching. We present a quantum algorithm for MWPM in general graphs that runs in \( widetildeO(n m^2/3log W) \) time, where W is an upper bound on the magnitude of the edge weights. This is an improvement over the best known classical combinatorial bound of \( widetildeO(m√ n log W) \) in the dense regime, where m≥n^(3/2). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantum algorithm to obtain an asymptotic improvement over the best classical combinatorial algorithm for the MWPM problem in general graphs. The running time of our method accounts for QRAM initialization and access overheads up to polylogarithmic factors, as well as all classical updates to the data structures. At a high level, our algorithm is based on a classical framework due to Duan, Pettie, and Su, but our algorithm requires replacing certain classical tasks with quantum methods, alternative analysis of classical procedures, and the use of alternative data structures that can be implemented effectively in the QRAM model.

items.title: Reducing the Entanglement Cost of Distributed Bipartite Quantum Computation with Constant Qubit Overhead
items.authors: Kosuke Matsui, Jun-Yi Wu, Min-Hsiu Hsieh, Mio Murao
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Every bipartite Clifford unitary is implementable via exact deterministic LOCC at the optimal entanglement lower bound lceillog₂OpSch(U)rceil Bell pairs using at most two auxiliary qubits per QPU. Non-Clifford unitaries with Clifford+T decompositions require at most 2t additional Bell pairs, where t is the T-count.
items.question: Can the operator Schmidt rank lower bound on entanglement cost for distributed bipartite unitaries be achieved with constant auxiliary qubit overhead per QPU?
items.prior: was (2n_A,2n_B) auxiliary qubits for Choi-state teleportation attaining log₂OpSch(U) Bell pairs (Eisert et al. 2000, Zhou et al. 2000)
items.limits: Deterministic exact LOCC with perfect shared Bell pairs; bipartite setting with at most two QPUs.
items.tools: operator Schmidt rank decomposition · symplectic matrix factorization · elementary block decomposition · mid-circuit measurement and qubit reuse
items.caption: Decomposition of a 4-qubit Clifford unitary into three elementary blocks (G₁, G₂, G₃) executed sequentially to achieve optimal entanglement consumption.
items.abstract: Distributed quantum computation connects multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through quantum communication to jointly perform large-scale quantum computations. Since the number of qubits available at each QPU is limited, it is important to reduce quantum communication while keeping the qubit overhead small. To this end, we study an entanglement-assisted model, in which entanglement consumption serves as a measure of quantum communication cost. For exact deterministic implementations in this model, the operator Schmidt rank of the target bipartite unitary provides a general lower bound on entanglement cost when qubit overhead is unrestricted. However, it has remained unclear how closely this bound can be approached with constant qubit overhead. In this work, we show that this lower bound is attainable for every bipartite Clifford unitary using at most two auxiliary qubits per QPU. In addition, for non-Clifford unitaries specified by exact Clifford+T decompositions with T-count t, we construct implementations with the same qubit overhead whose entanglement cost is at most 2t Bell pairs above this lower bound.

items.title: A Noise Operator Approach to Quantum Query Complexity and Time-Space Tradeoff Lower Bounds
items.authors: Paul Beame, Blake Holman, Niels Kornerup
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Proves fully general quantum query lower bound of Ω(n^(4/3)(loglogn)/(S^(1/3)logn)) for sorting n numbers from [n²] using at most S qubits, and Ω(nm/S) queries for computing almost all hash functions from strongly universal families mapping n bits to m bits.
items.question: Can unconditional time-space tradeoff lower bounds be proven for general (adaptive, non-output-oblivious) quantum sorting algorithms and universal hash families?
items.prior: Only output-oblivious sorting bounds were known: T = Ω(n^(3/2)/√S) (Klauck, Špalek, de Wolf 2003). For integer multiplication, prior quantum bound was Ω(n²/(Slogn)) (Beame, Kornerup, Whitmeyer 2024).
items.limits: Asymptotic regime for large n. Inputs drawn uniformly from [n²] for sorting and Dⁿ for linear algebra problems. S ≤c g / 17 for $(g, h, c)$-rigid matrix products.
items.tools: Noise operator method · Recording-query basis (compressed oracle) · Quantum noise stability bounds · Matrix rigidity analysis
items.abstract: Time and space (memory) are two of the most important measures of cost in computation, even more so for quantum computation. In quantum computation our tools for proving unconditional tradeoffs between time and space are surprisingly limited. The first quantum time-space tradeoff lower bounds were proven for sorting by Klauck, Špalek and de Wolf. Unfortunately, their method is limited to proving output-oblivious lower bounds (i.e. the lower bounds only apply to algorithms with a non-adaptive output schedule) and other methods have yielded nothing beyond output-oblivious lower bounds for sorting.We prove the first fully general quantum time-space tradeoff lower bound for sorting. We do so by introducing a novel method based on the noise operator to add to the analysis toolkit for proving quantum query and time space tradeoff lower bounds. By combining our resulting quantum noise stability bound with quantum recording query methods, we prove an Ω(n^(4/3) (loglogn)/(S^(1/3) logn)) lower bound on the number of queries that a fully general quantum algorithm with at most S qubits of memory requires to sort n numbers from [n²]. Applying our noise operator argument involves purely classical arguments, which makes it particularly simple to use. We also us it to prove that, for any strongly universal (pairwise independent) hash function family H from n bits to m bits, almost all hash functions in H require a quantum algorithm with at most S qubits of memory to make Ω(nm/S) queries to an input x in order to compute h(x), even with very small success probability. Previously, Mansour, Nisan, and Tiwari had shown a similar classical lower bound using their hash mixing lemma. Our noise operator method allows us to use a related but simpler property of hash functions to prove our lower bounds.

items.title: Verifiable Quantum Advantage and Computation via Quantum Circuit Obfuscation
items.authors: Alexandru Gheorghiu, Aparna Gupte, Vojtvech Havlívcek, Yunchao Liu
items.matched: sampling-based quantum advantage and its classical spoofing
items.result: Two-message, publicly and classically verifiable quantum-advantage protocol constructed from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qiO) for ancilla-free unitaries assuming BQPnot⊆i.o.BPP.
items.question: Can the security of peaked-circuit quantum advantage and classical verification of BQP be based on cryptographic quantum indistinguishability obfuscation?
items.limits: Requires quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for ancilla-free unitaries, BQPnot⊆i.o.BPP, and post-quantum one-way functions for public verification of BQP.
items.tools: quantum indistinguishability obfuscation · peaked random circuit sampling · worst-to-average-case reduction via local mixing · ancilla-free tidy circuit compilation
items.caption: Implication graph showing how quantum RIO, SCP, and qiO for ancilla-free and tidy circuits lead to private and public classical verification of BQP computations and verifiable quantum advantage.
items.abstract: We construct protocols for classically verifiable quantum advantage and classical verification of BQP computations using emphquantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qiO). Specifically, given qiO and assuming a slightly stronger version of BQP≠BPP, we construct a two-message quantum-advantage protocol that is efficiently and publicly verifiable. Our result can be viewed as a rigorous cryptographic foundation for the heuristic quantum advantage proposals based on emphpeaked random circuit sampling of Aaronson and Zhang (arXiv:2404.14493). We also construct two simple protocols for classically verifying arbitrary BQP computations. The first protocol is privately verifiable and assumes only the existence of qiO. This gives a rare example of a nontrivial cryptographic application of (quantum) iO that does not make additional computational hardness assumptions. The second protocol additionally assumes post-quantum one-way functions and is emphpublicly verifiable. To our knowledge, this is the first publicly verifiable protocol for classical verification of BQP computations under computational assumptions in the standard model. We show that all our results hold when qiO is assumed only for ancilla-free unitary circuits. As evidence supporting this assumption, we prove a worst-to-average-case reduction for obfuscating such circuits. This reduction extends the local-mixing framework of Canetti, Chamon, Mucciolo and Ruckenstein (TCC 2024) under quantum analogues of their assumptions.

items.title: Complex Quantum Dynamics Versus Classical Simulability of Noisy Random Circuits
items.authors: Anjali Waghmare, Sergii Strelchuk, Sathyawageeswar Subramanian
items.matched: Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation
items.result: Dynamical diagnostics (magic, scrambling, anticoncentration, non-Gaussianity) decouple from classical simulation hardness in noisy quantum circuits. Local depolarising noise damps fourth-order Pauli moments asymptotically twice as fast as second-order moments, causing magic to vanish at depth Θ(N) while efficient classical sampling threshold remains Θ(1) under sparse noise.
items.question: In noisy quantum circuits, do dynamical diagnostics such as magic, scrambling, and anticoncentration reliably track classical simulability?
items.limits: Depolarising noise on brickwork Clifford+T and Majorana dephasing on matchgate+SWAP circuits.
items.tools: fourth-order Clifford commutant · Pauli-path truncation · Majorana transfer matrix · replica transfer matrix
items.caption: Circuit depth versus depolarising noise parameter (or dephasing parameter). Dashed curves mark dynamical resource boundaries; solid colors mark fastest classical simulation algorithms, showing the dynamical boundary crosscuts classical simulation efficiency regions in both directions.
items.abstract: Claims of quantum advantage rest on the classical hardness of simulating quantum circuits. Magic, operator scrambling, anticoncentration, and non-Gaussianity for fermionic circuits are standard diagnostics of complex quantum dynamics. For pure states, some of these have been rigorously connected to classical simulability. Whether these diagnostics reliably track the limits of efficient classical simulation under noise remains unclear. Here, we show that in noisy Clifford+T and nearest-neighbour matchgate+SWAP circuits, dynamical diagnostics and classical simulability can separate in both directions. In particular, the diagnostics can remain nontrivial after classical simulation becomes efficient, or become trivial before known efficient classical algorithms apply. We trace this mismatch to the different statistical properties they probe: magic and scrambling depend on fourth-order statistics of the Pauli spectrum, whereas the simulation algorithms depend primarily on second-order moments, which local noise suppresses at different rates. Thus, dynamical diagnostics measured on a noisy quantum device do not by themselves constitute evidence for classical hardness.

items.authors: Azar C. Nakhl, Ben Harper, Muhammad Usman, Thomas Quella

items.result: AKLT ground and scar states exhibit high non-stabilizerness via Stabilizer Rényi Entropy despite low entanglement. Quenches to the Heisenberg Hamiltonian melt string order faster as bimagnon excitation number increases.

items.abstract: Clifford augmented methods have emerged as a powerful technique to simulate quantum circuits and many-body systems by exploiting the stabiliser structure found in said systems, whilst additionally enabling one to readily quantify the non-stabilizerness (i.e. magic) present. In this work, we utilise a qudit Clifford augmented simulation method to probe the presence of magic in the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) model, finding that its ground state and scar states are highly magical as quantified by their Stabiliser Rényi Entropy (SRE). Nevertheless, owing to its low entanglement structure, these states are still readily expressible as a Clifford augmented Matrix Product State with low bond-dimension and moreover may be time-evolved using the Clifford augmented time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) algorithm. We utilise Clifford augmented TDVP to study the string order dynamics in the scar states of the AKLT model after a quench within the Haldane phase to the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian. We observe that there is a decay of string order following the quench, which is more pronounced with increasing bimagnon number. This finding highlights the sensitivity of string order in the AKLT scar states to symmetry-preserving quenches, even when the initial and final Hamiltonians belong to the same topological phase.

items.title: Oscillator-Qubit Primitives for a Molecular Quantum Dynamics Simulator
items.authors: Jungsoo Hong, Joonsuk Huh
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Synthesizes nonlinear, multimode bosonic phase gates via generalized Jacobi–Anger expansions inside quantum signal processing, yielding multimode benchmark circuits about one-third shorter than direct Fourier quantum signal processing.
items.question: How can nonlinear and multimode bosonic phase gates for non-Born–Oppenheimer molecular quantum dynamics be synthesized near-optimally on oscillator-qubit devices without intermediate ancilla measurements or resets?
items.prior: Direct oscillator-qubit generalized quantum signal processing (OQ-GQSP) and trigonometric-gate-implemented Fourier synthesis (TGIFS); TGIFS required T_CD/τ_unit = 476 000 (symmetric) vs 52 000 here on a 1 ps CO₂ vibrational benchmark.
items.limits: Simulated rather than experimentally measured; short-window CO₂ simulation slightly misses coherence error criterion (0.050042 vs 0.05 threshold) under circuit QED noise at qubit and oscillator lifetimes near 2 ms and 5 ms; specific to declared nuclear-coordinate domains.
items.tools: quantum signal processing (QSP) · generalized Jacobi–Anger (GJA) expansion · circuit QED / trapped-ion noise model · Lindblad master equation
items.caption: Plots conditional-displacement time (in balanced query units τ_base) as a function of phase strength and precision, showing circuit cost scaling across different synthesis methods for single-tone and multimode targets.
items.abstract: Molecular quantum dynamics simulations that treat both electrons and nuclei quantum mechanically are crucial for predicting chemical reactions. With classical computation, a full wave-function representation of both types of particles requires resources that grow exponentially with their number. Oscillator-qubit processors, including trapped-ion and circuit QED devices, represent electronic states with qubits and nuclear vibrations with oscillators. Their native operations produce linear vibronic interactions, from which programmable anharmonic interactions can be built. Product-formula approaches build the corresponding phase gates by repeating small noncommuting phase steps, and quantum signal processing (QSP) approaches approximate each gate directly with a Fourier series. Simulations apply many such gates in sequence, so accumulated cost and error limit how long the dynamics can be followed. We propose near-optimal quantum primitives for molecular quantum dynamics simulation, covering the representations of both types of particles and their interactions. We synthesize nonlinear and multimode bosonic phase gates using generalized Jacobi-Anger (GJA) expansions within QSP, with a cost that grows near-optimally in both interaction strength and precision. Our interaction model and gate synthesis each have their own accuracy setting. Chosen together, these settings make our multimode benchmark circuits about one-third shorter than those of the previous direct QSP approach. We then simulate energy exchange between the stretching and bending vibrations of a simplified carbon dioxide model. With circuit-QED noise, a short simulation narrowly misses our accuracy criteria at qubit and oscillator lifetimes near 2 ms and 5 ms. These lifetimes mark a concrete checkpoint on the way to simulating anharmonic multimode molecular quantum dynamics on near-term oscillator-qubit processors.

items.title: Quantum--classical break-even in electronic dynamics of macrocyclic molecules
items.authors: Shu Kanno, Kenji Sugisaki, Takashi Imamichi, Toshinari Itoko, Rei Sakuma, Hajime Nakamura, Qi Gao, Naoki Yamamoto
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Quantum wall-clock runtime matches estimated classical HPC runtime (tens to hundreds of 36-core nodes) for nonequilibrium electronic dynamics of a 120-qubit [60]annulene ring model.
items.question: Can quantum hardware reach wall-clock break-even against practical classical computing resources for chemical electronic dynamics on periodic macrocycles?
items.limits: Restricted to 1D periodic Hamiltonians with short-range interactions; ignores small 3- and 4-center orbital overlap terms; assumes fixed electron-number parity sector for boundary Jordan–Wigner strings.
items.tools: Tensor-network circuit compression · Local Hilbert–Schmidt test (LHST) with channel–state duality · IBM superconducting quantum processors · Space-time gate replication
items.caption: Simulated and QPU-measured time evolution of local observables in 120-qubit [60]annulene versus classical simulation baselines, comparing both physical accuracy and execution runtime.
items.abstract: Here we demonstrate quantum--classical break-even for chemical dynamics applications, reaching useful accuracy with a quantum-hardware wall-clock time comparable to that estimated for practical classical computing resources. Specifically, we construct a quantum workflow for electronic dynamics based on tensor-network circuit compression leveraging spatial locality, extending circuit compression beyond one-dimensional open-boundary systems. This enables application of the workflow to problems that are hardware-native but classically hard. The workflow targets one-dimensional periodic Hamiltonians: circuits classically optimized only for short-time evolution within a small spatial region can be replicated in both space and time to construct long-time dynamics of the full system without classically simulating the corresponding large-scale evolution. We apply the workflow to cyclic conjugated macrocycles with rotational periodicity, 12-qubit benzene and 120-qubit [60]annulene, by embedding their electronic structure onto loops of IBM quantum processors. For the annulene, the quantum-processing-unit (QPU) wall-clock times for hole-doped nonequilibrium dynamics became comparable to the estimated wall-clock time of two classical methods, Majorana propagation and matrix-product-state time evolution based on the time-dependent variational principle; this corresponds to tens to hundreds of compute nodes depending on the task (36 CPU cores per node), assuming near-ideal parallel scaling, bringing the quantum calculation into a wall-clock-time regime comparable to conventional parallel high-performance-computing resources. We also show a situation in which a hybrid quantum--classical calculation is a reasonable choice in terms of both accuracy and computational time. These results show that quantum hardware can become a realistic computational option for chemically relevant electronic dynamics.

items.title: No-go theorems for dual Hamiltonians of Non-Abelian Lattice Gauge Theories
items.authors: Marco Garofalo, Tobias Hartung, Timo Jakobs, Paul Ludwig, Johann Ostmeyer, Carsten Urbach
items.matched: lattice gauge theory simulation on quantum hardware
items.result: Canonical reparametrisation of non-Abelian Kogut-Susskind lattice Hamiltonians into dual plaquette variables inevitably yields non-local operator strings whose interaction distance scales as Ω(ℓ) with lattice extent ℓ. Attempting to retain locality via auxiliary helper links and dynamic plaquette constraints fails because the constraints do not close into an algebra and overconstrain states to ψ(widetildeU₁, widetildeU₂) = const.
items.question: Can the Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian for non-Abelian lattice gauge theories be transformed into a dual formulation with a free magnetic term and strictly local interactions?
items.prior: Dual plaquette formulations in U(1) lattice gauge theory yield local next-neighbour interactions in the electric Hamiltonian with a free magnetic term.
items.limits: Pure gauge SU(N) theory on spatial lattices of dimension d > 1, preserving degrees of freedom and fundamental canonical commutators under static or dynamic constraints.
items.tools: Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian · dual reparametrisation · maximal spanning tree on dual lattice · Lie algebra commutators
items.caption: (a) The choice of static constraint found in [ 6 ] .
items.abstract: Hamiltonian simulations of lattice gauge theories promise new insights into the inner workings of QCD. The rapid development of quantum computing hardware suggests that large scale simulations may soon become feasible. However, no efficient formulation suitable for simulations near the continuum limit is currently known for the non-Abelian case, and existing candidates typically feature long range interactions in the electric part of the Hamiltonian. We prove that such non- localities are unavoidable when the gauge configuration is reparametrised while preserving both the number of degrees of freedom and the fundamental commutation relations. We then attempt to mitigate this by introducing additional gauge links alongside additional constraints. Although this approach is successful in U(1), we prove that the corresponding construction is inconsistent for non-Abelian lattice gauge theories.

items.abstract: Imaginary-time evolution can be reconstructed from real-time quantum simulations using exact integral transforms. We identify the construction of Guo, Shibu, Lin, and Zhao as a continuous linear combination of Hamiltonian simulations and show that its slow 1/t_cut convergence arises from a redundant kernel component. We extend the construction from pure-state matrix elements to thermal traces and correlators. One real-time dataset then reconstructs targeted inverse temperatures, Euclidean separations, and chemical potentials through classical post-processing, bringing finite-(T,θ,μ) physics within reach of real-time quantum simulation without thermal-state preparation. We benchmark the method on one- and two-flavor lattice Schwinger models, including circuit-level simulations with depolarizing noise.
