items.abstract: Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of O(deg(V_loc) n^(deg(V_loc)) + 8Lnn_atomχ² + 2n²), where deg(V_loc) is the degree of the polynomial local potential, n_atom is the number of atoms in the system, L is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and n is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.

items.result: Characterizes multivariate quantum signal processing (MQSP) via multiport IIR transfer functions. Achieves multi-oracle Hamiltonian simulation under H=∑_j H_j with query cost ≈t⟨vecλ,vecC⟩_(1/2)+O(|vecC|₁log(1/ε)) and optimal sparse simulation query cost Θ(√d|H|_(1→2)t) with additive error dependence.
items.question: Can quantum signal processing and quantum singular value transformation be generalized to implement multivariate matrix transformations of multiple noncommuting, nonnormal block-encoded operators?
items.limits: Analytic bounds hold uniformly across oracle promises; requires block encodings of input matrices.
items.tools: multivariate quantum signal processing · multiport infinite-impulse-response (IIR) filters · transfer function methodology · block encoding
items.abstract: We develop Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing for designing matrix-valued transformations of multiple noncommuting nonnormal block-encoded matrices. Our framework equips quantum transducers with the analytic structure of multiport Infinite-Impulse-Response (IIR) filters and establishes a transfer-function methodology for designing quantum query algorithms. Efficiently computable analytic bounds that hold uniformly across the oracle promise yield efficient quantum circuits with logarithmic error dependence and near-unity success probability, paralleling the approximation-theoretic guarantees of univariate QSP/QSVT. We provide a complete characterization of achievable transfer functions and a principled library of analytic IIR components. Our modular designs greatly improve or resolve the per-oracle query complexity of open multi-oracle problems: (1) Hamiltonian simulation under H=∑_j H_j with weighted quasinorm cost ≈t⟨vecλ,vecC⟩_(1/2)+O(|vecC|₁log(1/ε)) for block-encoding normalizations vecλ and costs vecC; (2) sparse simulation with optimal time--norm Θ(√d|H|_(1→2)t) and additive error dependence; (3) solving linear systems and (4) differential equations under minimal matrix assumptions with optimal weighted state-preparation and multi-term cost; (5) ground-state preparation and energy estimation; (6) generalized eigenvalue problems. We apply these to exactly simulate downfolded Hamiltonians with leading cost t⟨vecλ_eff,vecC_eff⟩_(1/2) further reduced by fractional dynamic correlation energy contributions from coarse-grained Hamiltonians, and show similar classical-data-input-reduction results for multiscale graph classification via Kron reduction. We also show the online generalization with anisotropic Kalman filtering of streaming quantum data.

items.title: Near-Optimal Ground-State Preparation without Controlled Hamiltonian Evolutions
items.authors: Dhrumil Patel, Steven T. Flammia, Raul Garcia-Patron

items.result: Ground-state preparation requires only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolutions U_H = e^(-iHτ) and U_H^† with query complexity widetildeO(α_H / (γ√η)). This matches the lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors without requiring controlled Hamiltonian evolution.
items.question: Can the near-optimal complexity of ground-state preparation be achieved using only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution instead of controlled Hamiltonian evolution?
items.prior: Required widetildeO(α_H / (γ√η)) queries to ctrl-U_H or block encodings (Lin & Tong 2020; Dong et al. 2022).
items.limits: Spectral norm bound |H| ≤α_H, known spectral gap lower bound E₁ - E₀ ≥γ> 0, overlap lower bound ⟨φ₀|ψ⟩⟨ψ|φ₀⟩≥η> 0, and coherent query access to state preparation U_ψ.
items.tools: spectral descent principle · shifted SWAP echo · Laurent quantum signal processing (QSP) · fixed-point amplitude amplification (FPAA)
items.caption: Quantum circuit schematic for the t-th stage of Coherent Spectral Descent (CSD), showing coherent witness subspace amplification followed by a witness measurement and anchor update.
items.abstract: Ground-state preparation, energy estimation, and property estimation are fundamental tasks in quantum simulation. Existing ground-state preparation algorithms achieve near-optimal complexity using block encodings or controlled Hamiltonian evolution, raising a natural question: is controlled Hamiltonian evolution necessary, or can the same scaling be attained in the weaker access model that provides access to only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution? We resolve this question by giving two algorithms that access the input Hamiltonian H only through queries to U_H and its inverse U_H^†, where |H|≤α_H and τ=Θ(1/α_H). Given an input state with ground-state weight at least η and a spectral gap of H of at least γ, our first algorithm uses fresh copies of the input state and requires widetildeO(α_H/(γη)) queries to U_H and U_H^†, while our second algorithm uses coherent access to the input-state preparation unitary and its inverse to improve this complexity to widetildeO(α_H/(γ√η)). The latter bound matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors, showing that algorithms with additional access to controlled Hamiltonian evolution cannot improve the query complexity for ground-state preparation beyond logarithmic factors. Both algorithms are based on a simple mechanism that we call the spectral descent principle, in which the algorithm starts from the input state |ψ⟩ and progressively descends through the energy spectrum, moving closer to the ground state until the desired fidelity is reached. We also extend this framework to ground-state property and energy estimation and give explicit complexity guarantees for both tasks.

items.title: Less precise but less noisy: local circuits for momentum-space state preparation and measurement
items.authors: Etienne Granet, Henrik Dreyer
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Adiabatic state preparation reaches lower energies than Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT) on noisy hardware for tight-binding chains with Ngtrapprox20 qubits at equal two-qubit gate counts. Noise heating per two-qubit gate scales as O(1) for FFT but remains constant O(1/N) for adiabatic evolution.
items.question: How does circuit noise sensitivity compare between high-precision Fermionic Fourier Transforms and local Hamiltonian simulation or adiabatic evolution for state preparation and measurement?
items.prior: FFT state preparation and momentum measurement (Ref [31]) exhibited high noise sensitivity due to global error propagation.
items.limits: Antiperiodic boundary conditions, tight-binding free-fermion chains, non-post-selected initial state |+...+⟩ introducing tiny energy shifts scaling as 1/N, fixed number of measurement shots (300 to 375).
items.tools: Quantinuum System Model H2-2 trapped-ion processor · Adiabatic evolution Trotter circuits · Momentum Distribution from Local Measurements (MDLM) · Jordan-Wigner transformation
items.caption: Measured energy density and energy increase per two-qubit gate versus system size N for FFT and adiabatic evolution on Quantinuum H2-2. Shows adiabatic evolution achieving lower energies than FFT above N≈20 due to constant heating per gate compared to linear growth for FFT.
items.abstract: Quantum algorithms are usually optimized for gate count or circuit depth. We find on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer that for a tight-binding chain ground state preparation, there is a system size N beyond which the adiabatic evolution reaches significantly lower energies than the Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT), with the same number of gates, and with the same circuit depth. We attribute this high noise sensitivity of the FFT to its high precision, being able to distinguish momenta by 1/N. This high resolution in momentum space requires long-range couplings in real space, which propagates errors faster. In contrast, although local and physical circuits such as the adiabatic evolution have a coarser momentum resolution, they also propagate errors more slowly. For physical applications, high momentum resolution is rarely required and is often worth trading for low noise sensitivity. We also introduce a momentum measurement scheme that although less precise than FFT, is less costly and less noisy. We show that it achieves better performance than FFT for spectral function measurement on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer. Our work emphasizes the importance of reducing the noise sensitivity of quantum algorithms, beyond the number of gates or circuit depth.

items.title: Molecular Dynamics with Nuclear Effects on Quantum Computers
items.authors: Lukas Haßfurth, Juliane Heitkämper, Elias Walter, Birger Horstmann
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Hybrid quantum-classical NEO-VQE algorithm propagates Born-Oppenheimer dynamics including nuclear quantum effects, achieving under 5 % average vibrational frequency error on H₂, H₂O, and H₅O₂⁺ using 5 to 7 active orbitals (about 10 qubits).
items.question: How can nuclear quantum effects be incorporated into ab initio molecular dynamics calculations using near-term quantum algorithms?
items.limits: Simulated noiseless quantum circuits (classical emulation); only selected protons treated quantum-mechanically; canonical orbital basis rather than natural orbitals; hardware-efficient ansatzes fail on nonlinear couplings in the Zundel ion.
items.tools: nuclear-electronic orbital (NEO) framework · variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) · velocity Verlet integration · Hartree-Fock active-space embedding · UCCSD and hardware-efficient ansatzes
items.caption: Simulated NEO vibrational power spectrum (with s and p_z nuclear orbitals) of the Zundel ion versus DFT harmonic modes and experimental Ar/Ne-tagged predissociation spectra across 500--4000cm⁻¹.
items.abstract: Nuclear quantum effects are critical for describing proton transfer and hydrogen bonding, but their incorporation into quantum chemistry calculations is often computationally prohibitive on classical hardware. A promising alternative are quantum computers due to their linear scaling in the space requirements with system size. We introduce a novel hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for ab-initio molecular dynamics that incorporates nuclear quantum effects via the nuclear-electronic orbital method. The proposed algorithm evaluates ground state energies and forces on the quantum computer using a variational quantum eigensolver, while the molecular geometries are updated classically. We validate our approach through simulations of H₂, H₂O and the Zundel ion H₅O₂⁺, comparing the simulated vibrational spectra with experimental data. Upon inclusion of nuclear quantum effects, the proton shuttling movement in the Zundel ion becomes effectively barrierless, and errors in the simulated frequencies improve significantly. Employing compact hardware-efficient ansatz circuits we achieve results comparable to the more accurate UCCSD ansatzes, which hints towards the feasibility of executing our algorithm on near-term quantum devices.

items.title: First-quantized quantum simulation with non-local potentials by matrix-product-state encoding
items.authors: Kazuki Tsuoka, Taichi Kosugi, Masari Watanabe, Hirofumi Nishi, Yu-ichiro Matsushita
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Matrix product state encoding of non-local pseudopotentials yields a single Trotter step circuit depth of O(°(V_loc) n^(°(V_loc)) + 8Lnn_atomχ² + 2n²). For n = 7 qubits, depth is 1,747 versus 23,775 for direct unitary decomposition.
items.question: How to efficiently implement arbitrary non-local pseudopotentials within first-quantized quantum chemistry dynamics circuits?
items.prior: Direct dense unitary decomposition scaled exponentially as O(4ⁿ), reaching circuit depth 23,775 at n = 7.
items.limits: Demonstrated for a one-dimensional single-electron hydrogen ionization model in momentum representation. Assumes polynomial local potential V_loc and low bond dimension saturation for smooth projectors.
items.tools: matrix product state encoding · first-order Trotterization · binary-encoded wave functions · Qiskit transpiler unitary synthesis
items.caption: Circuit depth of a single Trotter step plotted against qubit count n for MPS bond dimensions χ= 2, 4, 6, 8 compared to standard unitary decomposition.
items.abstract: Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of O(deg(V_loc) n^(deg(V_loc)) + 8Lnn_atomχ² + 2n²), where deg(V_loc) is the degree of the polynomial local potential, n_atom is the number of atoms in the system, L is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and n is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.

items.title: Quantum impurity models: easy at equilibrium, universal in motion
items.authors: Srinivasan Arunachalam, Sergey Bravyi, Anirban Chowdhury, Arkopal Dutt, Alexandru Gheorghiu, Zhi Li
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Ground energy of n-mode fermionic impurity models with constant impurity size m is classically computable to error ε in poly(n, 1/ε) time; Helmholtz free energy and thermofield double state take poly(n, β, 1/ε) time at inverse temperature β. Simulating time evolution e^(-iHt) is BQP-complete.
items.question: Can equilibrium properties of quantum impurity models be calculated in polynomial classical time, and can time-independent constant-size impurity models simulate universal quantum computation?
items.prior: Classical ground energy algorithm runtime was poly(n)exp[O(mlog³(m/ε))] (Bravyi and Gosset 2017); universality was known only for time-dependent impurity models or impurity size scaling with n.
items.limits: Impurity must have constant size m = O(1); interaction norm satisfies |V| ≤poly(n) (or |V| ≤1 for constructive thermofield double).
items.tools: Shelled Krylov decomposition · Fermionic Gaussian state approximations · Thermofield double purification · Wavepacket scattering encoding
items.caption: Two-stage reduction showing a quantum circuit compiled into sequential interactions with a stationary register, then mapped into the time evolution of a constant-size impurity model coupled to a free fermion bath.
items.abstract: A quantum impurity model describes a small interacting subsystem embedded into a large bath of free fermions. Here we study the computational complexity of calculating the ground energy, thermal equilibrium, and dynamical properties of these models. Our work reveals a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated by classical means, whereas time evolution can implement a universal quantum computation. More precisely, let H be the Hamiltonian of an impurity model with n fermionic modes and a constant-size impurity. We show that: (1) the ground energy of H can be approximated to additive error ε by a classical algorithm with runtime textsfpoly(n,1/ε), improving on the quasi-polynomial runtime of the best previously known algorithm; (2) at inverse temperature β, the Helmholtz free energy and a classical description of the thermofield double state can be computed to precision ε in time textsfpoly(n,β,1/ε); (3) simulating the time evolution e^(-iHt) is textsfBQP-complete, for H that is time-independent and has a fixed, constant impurity size. Our algorithms exploit exponential suppression of multi-particle bath excitations in a basis organized by energy scale and Krylov depth. Our universality construction realizes a stationary quantum processor whose program arrives in a stream of freely propagating fermions.

items.title: Toward Optimal Circuit Depth for Geometrically Local Hamiltonian Simulation
items.authors: Zhenyu Shen, Yusen Wu, Penghui Yao, Xiao Yuan, Yukun Zhang
items.matched: analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…
items.result: Nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulates n-qubit, time-independent, finite-range lattice Hamiltonians for time T≥1 to error ε with circuit depth O(Tlog(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nTlog(nT/ε)). Proves matching unconditional depth lower bound Ω(logn/loglogn) for uniform XXZ dynamics at fixed T and ε.
items.question: Can geometrically local Hamiltonian dynamics be simulated on a lattice with circuit depth and gate count that depend only logarithmically on system size, time, and target accuracy?
items.prior: Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low (2021) achieved circuit depth O(Tpolylog(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nTpolylog(nT/ε)).
items.limits: Fixed spatial dimension D, normalized local interaction strength J≤1, fixed-range interactions, exact single-qubit gates and nearest-neighbor CNOTs with bounded ancilla density per site.
items.tools: Lieb-Robinson spatial decomposition · corrected constant-order product formulas · concurrent control transport via snake routing · causal cone Lieb-Robinson lower-bound probes
items.caption: Circuit structure for block simulation showing label PREPARE, prefix arithmetic, phase distribution, and concurrent local data gate application across the logarithmic-diameter block.
items.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum systems is a central goal of quantum simulation. For geometrically local Hamiltonians, locality suggests that digital simulation should retain much of the parallelism of the underlying dynamics. For a target accuracy ε, we construct a nearest-neighbor quantum circuit that simulates the dynamics of an n-qubit, time-independent, finite-range Hamiltonian with normalized local interaction strength on a fixed-dimensional lattice for time T≥1, with circuit depth O(Tlog(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nTlog(nT/ε)). This reduces the polylogarithmic overhead of Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low to a single logarithm. On logarithmic-scale blocks from the Lieb--Robinson decomposition, a shallow but highly accurate implementation is essential for reducing the circuit depth. Our key observation is that spatial localization also controls the cost of high precision. In each block, the error of a constant-order product formula is compensated for by a correction, yielding exponential accuracy. The correction can be implemented with depth proportional to the block diameter, introducing no additional asymptotic depth scale beyond that required by spatial localization. Furthermore, we prove an unconditional circuit-depth lower bound for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians: at fixed evolution time T in the stated regime and sufficiently small fixed error ε, any nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulating these dynamics requires depth Ω(logn/loglogn). This matches our O(logn) upper bound up to a doubly logarithmic factor, establishing near-optimal circuit depth for lattice Hamiltonian simulation in this regime. Together, these results clarify the role of locality and precision in determining the circuit complexity of quantum dynamics and suggest broader principles for spatially constrained quantum computation.

items.title: Floquet-Universal Hamiltonian Simulation
items.authors: Emilio Onorati, Harriet Apel, Michael M. Wolf, Toby Cubitt
items.matched: analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…
items.result: A set of interactions S Floquet-simulates every target Hamiltonian in Lie(S) using physical interaction amplitudes with ratios bounded between 1 and 2, with frequencies bounded by poly(n) for k-local Hamiltonians whose intersection graph has chromatic number χ= O(1).
items.question: Which time-independent target Hamiltonians can be simulated by periodically driven Floquet Hamiltonians under bounded interaction strengths?
items.prior: Time-independent analogue simulation required polynomially scaling multi-scale interaction strength ratios (Cubitt, Montanaro, Piddock 2018).
items.limits: Frequency range scales exponentially with system size for general Hamiltonians lacking succinct descriptions; simulation runtime N periods scales as poly(n).
items.tools: Floquet theory · Magnus expansion truncation bounds · Lie algebra polynomial decomposition · Graph vertex colouring · Residue calculus
items.abstract: Analogue and digital Hamiltonian simulation represent two distinct approaches to making one quantum system replicate the physical properties of another, with consequences ranging from practical applications to complexity theory and quantum gravity. They are rooted in two distinct regimes of quantum dynamics: time-independent Hamiltonians for the former; fully controllable time-dependent quantum circuits in the latter. Time-periodic Hamiltonians represent an intermediate regime. In this work, we establish a theory of Floquet simulation where we use periodically driven Hamiltonians to synthesise time-independent ones. We show that a set of interactions S can Floquet-simulate every Hamiltonian in the Lie algebra Lie(S), and consequently we give a complete and constructive characterisation of Floquet-universal Hamiltonians that are able to produce any target Hamiltonian. Notably, our construction uses only O(1) local interaction strengths and ratios thereof, avoiding the impractical multi-scale local interaction strengths often required in analogue simulation via time-independent Hamiltonians. Instead, the construction requires a range of driving frequencies which scales polynomially with system size for important classes such as k-local lattice Hamiltonians. This has immediate complexity-theoretic implications, including numerous BQP-completeness and QMA-hardness results for natural physical properties and quantities studied in Floquet physics.

items.title: Polynomial-time classical and quantum simulation of quantum impurity models
items.authors: Jiaqing Jiang, Nathan Ju, Ojas Parekh, Chaithanya Rayudu, Andrew Zhao
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Ground-state energy and thermal partition function Z = tr(e^(-βH)) of quantum impurity models are classically computable in poly(n, δ⁻¹) and poly(n, β, δ⁻¹) time respectively.
items.question: Are quantum impurity models fundamentally classically tractable to simulate in static regimes, and can they provide superpolynomial quantum speedup?
items.prior: Quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm for ground-state energy estimation (Bravyi & Gosset 2017).
items.limits: Impurity size m = O(1) with arbitrary interaction; free noninteracting bath.
items.tools: Bandwise Krylov representation · Subspace compression lemma · Continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo · Quantum belief propagation
items.caption: One-dimensional block-coupling structure generated by transforming the noninteracting bath single-particle space into a Krylov basis.
items.abstract: Quantum impurity models are paradigmatic models of interacting quantum matter, as well as key computational primitives for modern electronic-structure methods. They describe a small subsystem of interacting fermions coupled to a large, noninteracting bath. We perform a comprehensive study of the computational complexity of simulating impurity models, delineating the boundary between classical and quantum tractability for this class of problems. Our main finding is that static properties of quantum impurity models can be calculated efficiently on a classical computer. Specifically, we give classical algorithms that (1) estimate the ground-state energy to additive precision δ in time poly(n,δ⁻¹), and (2) estimate the partition function at inverse temperature β to relative precision δ in time poly(n,β,δ⁻¹), where n is the system size. These results improve the previous best-known complexity for ground-state energy estimation from quasipolynomial to polynomial time, while establishing for the first time rigorous polynomial-time guarantees for simulating impurity models in thermal equilibrium. On the other hand, we find that simulating dynamical properties of impurity models is hard for classical computers but easy on a quantum computer. As a canonical example, we show that computing their nonequilibrium Green's functions captures the full power of quantum computation, even at finite temperature. Taken together, our results rule out superpolynomial quantum speedups for computing static properties, but provide an avenue for quantum advantage in simulating impurity physics out of equilibrium.

items.title: Sublinear-depth Quantum Simulation of Electrons with Atomic Orbitals
items.authors: Jakob Günther, Aram W. Harrow
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Single Trotter step for atomic orbital Hamiltonians implemented in depth O(polylog(N)) without ancillas, achieving sublinear simulation depth and total gate count N^(5/3 + o(1)).
items.question: Can quantum simulation of electronic structure using atomic orbital bases match the low circuit depth and gate count scalings achieved by plane-wave and real-space representations?
items.prior: Atomic orbital Trotter steps typically required deep circuits due to up to O(N⁴) interaction terms with irregular spatial structure, trailing plane-wave and grid basis scalings.
items.limits: Assumes a constant number of orbitals per atom, fixed minimum interatomic separation, and asymptotic regime in orbital number N.
items.tools: exponentially localized atomic orbitals · Fast Multipole Method (FMM) hierarchical decomposition · quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits · Trotter error bounds
items.abstract: Discretizing electronic degrees of freedom into atomic orbitals is the default choice to accurately model electrons in molecules in a compact and flexible way. We consider the task of simulating such electronic structure models on a quantum computer for N orbitals, keeping the number of orbitals per atom constant. Atomic orbitals give rise to Hamiltonians with potentially up to O(N⁴) terms and little structure, which made it challenging to match the complexity of methods based on plane waves and real-space grids. In this work, we show that a Trotter step for atomic orbitals can be implemented in depth O(polylog(N)) without ancillas by combining a rigorous treatment of orbital localization, a hierarchical Hamiltonian decomposition based on the Fast Multipole Method, and shallow quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits. By bounding the Trotter error, we obtain sublinear simulation depth, and our total gate count N^(5/3 + o(1)) matches the best scaling known for any basis.

items.title: Gate Dispersive Charge Detection in Ge/SiGe Quantum Dots
items.authors: M. R. Tanvir, E. Sajadi, M. Veldhorst, G. Scappucci, J. Salfi
items.matched: Silicon quantum electronics
items.result: Single hole box (SHB) assisted gate-dispersive readout enhances the (1,1) to (2,0) interdot power signal-to-noise ratio twenty-fold over direct gate-dispersive sensing (from 18.5±3 to 372±12 at integration time t_m=50ms), cutting unity-SNR integration time from 2.7ms to 135μs.
items.question: Can compact RF gate-dispersive readout detect charge and interdot transitions in planar Ge/SiGe quantum dots?
items.limits: SNR is constrained by substrate/dielectric dissipative loss degrading resonator impedance matching; optimal drive power is -95dBm; SHB in this device is an unintentional auxiliary dot.
items.tools: planar Ge/SiGe double quantum dot · 540 MHz RF gate-dispersive reflectometry · 350 nH superconducting NbTiN spiral inductor · single hole box (SHB) charge sensor

items.abstract: Spin qubits are an attractive platform for scalable quantum information processing, and recently, laterally gated quantum dots (QDs) in Ge heterostructures have emerged as a leading implementation of spin qubits. To date, RF single-hole transistors (SHT) and integrated superconducting resonators have been used for spin and charge readout, but their size can pose challenges. Here we demonstrate compact RF gate-dispersive charge readout of a Ge double QD (DQD), and a single hole box (SHB)-DQD system. We resolve QD loading and interdot transitions with both techniques. We find that the SHB enhances the interdot signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of our 540 MHz circuit by a factor of 20 for a DQD coupling t_c ≈5 GHz, providing a unity-SNR at 135 microseconds, c.f. for 2.7 miliseconds for the direct detection. Power- and temperature-dependent measurements verify that SNR is limited by dielectric loss which compromises impedance matching. These results establish a compact readout approach based on gate-dispersive detection for Ge/SiGe heterostructure QDs.

items.title: Flux- and tunnel-parity-controlled Josephson nonreciprocity from singlet-triplet competition in a parallel double quantum dot
items.authors: Debika Debnath, Fernando Dominguez, Patrik Recher
items.matched: exchange gates and two-qubit operations in semiconductor double quantum dots
items.result: Orbital flux and gauge-invariant tunnel parity P=±1 control singlet, triplet, and doublet many-body branch competition in a parallel double-dot Josephson junction in the strong-coupling regime U/Δ≫1, producing nonreciprocal diode efficiencies approaching η=40% near charge boundaries and 10--15% within the triplet sector.
items.question: How do orbital magnetic flux and tunnel-sign parity control nonreciprocal Josephson currents across many-body spin and charge crossovers in a strongly interacting parallel double quantum dot?
items.limits: Zero-bandwidth superconducting leads, interdot direct tunneling τ₁₂=0, interdot Coulomb repulsion U₁₂=0, single-level quantum dots.
items.tools: Zero-bandwidth BCS lead Hamiltonian · Exact diagonalization · Fourth-order perturbation theory of non-local cotunneling and exchange · Peierls phase substitution
items.caption: Diode efficiency η plotted as a function of quantum dot level energy ε₁ and loop flux Φ/Φ₀ for even (P=1) and odd (P=-1) tunnel parity. Nonreciprocity emerges around phase-shifted crossings of singlet, triplet, and doublet spectral branches.
items.abstract: Nonreciprocal supercurrents in interacting nanostructures can arise when the positive and negative critical currents probe inequivalent portions of a phase-dependent many-body spectrum. We study this mechanism in a parallel double-quantum-dot Josephson junction with strong intradot Coulomb repulsion, where local and non-local Cooper-pair transfer coexist. Using exact diagonalization of a zero-bandwidth Hamiltonian with explicit superconducting orbitals, we show that orbital flux and the gauge-invariant tunnel-sign parity control the interference between local Josephson processes and non-local exchange. For detuned dots, this produces flux-tunable singlet, triplet, and doublet ground-state spectral branches and two rectification regimes. Near the boundaries of the charge sector with singly occupied dots [(1,1) sector], doublet branches compete with singlet or triplet branches, yielding diode efficiencies approaching 40%. Within the triplet-dominated (1,1) sector, nearby singlet crossings asymmetrically reshape the ground-state envelope even when both critical-current extrema lie on the triplet-like branch, producing a broader response of order 10-15%. Finite temperature generally suppresses charge-crossover rectification, however, for intermediate temperatures we find an enhancement of both the normalized efficiency and the absolute critical-current asymmetry in the triplet regime. These results establish phase-dependent many-body branch competition as a gate-, flux-, and tunnel-parity-sensitive source of Josephson nonreciprocity.

items.title: Nonlinear collective-spin dynamics for quantum-enhanced sensing in solid-state platforms
items.authors: Le Bin Ho
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Connects nonlinear collective-spin twisting dynamics to solid-state platforms, surveying spin squeezing and quantum enhancements across NV ensembles (demonstrating -0.50±0.13 dB squeezing or 6.7(6)% amplification), donor spins in ²⁸Si, and magnetic Kittel modes.
items.question: How do microscopic interactions, disorder, and decoherence dictate the generation of quantum-enhanced metrological states via nonlinear collective-spin dynamics in solid-state platforms?
items.limits: Spatial disorder and inhomogeneous couplings break collective permutation symmetry; technical noise, control errors, and decoherence cap effective nonlinear interaction time.
items.tools: Dicke basis collective spin formalism · one-axis and two-axis twisting (OAT/TAT) · Floquet pulse engineering · nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center ensembles · tqix simulation package
items.caption: Wineland squeezing parameter ξ² plotted against scaled evolution time χt, comparing noise reduction capabilities of one-axis twisting, two-axis twisting, and two-axis non-twisting dynamics.
items.abstract: Collective spin systems in solid-state materials are promising platforms for quantum-enhanced sensing. In systems such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, donor spins in silicon, and magnetic materials, interactions among many spins can generate collective quantum correlations that improve measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit. This tutorial develops an intuitive, materials-oriented framework for understanding these effects through nonlinear collective-spin dynamics. We show how nonlinear interactions reshape collective spin states in phase space, redistribute quantum fluctuations, and generate metrologically useful states such as spin-squeezed and entangled states. We then connect these ideal collective dynamics to microscopic interactions and realistic solid-state systems, discussing how interaction strength, disorder, decoherence, and experimental control affect sensing performance. Different platforms and experiments are compared to highlight key material properties, advantages, and limitations. The tutorial focuses on a materials-oriented understanding of nonlinear collective-spin sensing, rather than a comprehensive comparison of experimental platforms or a practical guide to sensing experiments.

items.title: Phonon interference induced by defect pairs
items.authors: Ran-Bo Yang, Ming-Hao Li, Chun-Yu Cai, Yue-Wen Wang, Zhi-Qing Li, Li-Xia Zhao, Zi-Wu Wang
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Real-space lattice-wave interference driven by defect pairs can be quantitatively described using the local Huang-Rhys factor S, yielding interference geometry tunable into Dirac-like and nodal-line states via defect spacing, depth, and localization.
items.question: How can single-mode coherent phonon interference launched by localized electron-phonon coupling at defects be described and mapped in real space?
items.limits: Theoretical model assuming monoclinic HfO₂ parameters, a single selected optical phonon mode (ω_k = 76THz, k = 7.8nm⁻¹), and negligible multi-mode mixing over the coherence duration.
items.tools: Huang-Rhys model · Fröhlich electron-phonon interaction Hamiltonian · Quantum defect model · Ultrafast optical emission spectrum simulations
items.caption: Spatial maps of phonon interference fringes and integrated Huang-Rhys factors S as functions of energy-level depth ratio E₂/E₁, localization ratio β₁/β₂, and defect spacing D, showing transitions into Dirac-like and nodal-line destructive interference patterns.
items.abstract: The coherent dynamics of lattice waves is of significant importance for exploring the nonadiabatic phenomena of the electron-phonon coupling under nonequilibrium conditions. Here, we propose a theoretical model for phonon interference induced by a defect pair, in which lattice waves with the selective modes are launched independently by each of defects due to the strongly local electron-phonon coupling. We find that the intensities of phonon interference fringes could be directly evaluated by a measurable quantity in experiments--Huang-Rhys factor, and the geometry of interference patterns could be modified by the internal parameters of defect pair, including the charge states, spatial distance, energy-level depth and localization strength. In particular, several novel quantum states, such as the Dirac-like and nodal-line topological states are emerged for the appropriate internal parameters. Furthermore, using Huang-Rhys model, we simulate the ultrafast optical spectroscopy in the phonon interference duration when defect pairs are excited as the color centers, where interference fringes are perfectly matched by intensities of spectrum, similar to the lock-key pattern. These results show that defect pair, serving as the driven force for the coherent dynamical processes for multidegrees of freedom, offers an ideal platform to explore fundamental quantum phenomena in nonequilibrium and ultrafast physics.

items.title: Thin-capping layer epitaxial quantum dots for near-field quantum photonics
items.authors: Yuting Guo, Jonathan Bar-David, Pasquale Cilibrizzi, Sung-Yul L. Park, Jin Dong Song, Luca Sapienza
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: InAs/GaAs quantum dots with a 10 nm GaAs capping layer achieve emission linewidths down to 0.13 nm and exciton lifetimes of 0.9-1.1 ns, matching 95 nm capped baselines.
items.question: Can epitaxial InAs/GaAs quantum dots maintain high optical coherence and lifetime when placed within 10-20 nm of the surface for near-field coupling?
items.prior: Wang et al. (2017) reported 65 ps lifetime and 0.65 nm extrapolated linewidth for 10 nm capping layers; Guimaraes et al. (2018) reported 0.14 nm for 20 nm capping layers.
items.limits: Measured at ∼17 K under non-resonant 880 nm pulsed excitation; system spectral resolution limit is 0.04 nm.
items.tools: molecular beam epitaxy · two-step capping layer growth with thermal interrupt · micro-photoluminescence spectroscopy · time-correlated single-photon counting with SNSPDs
items.caption: Narrowest emission linewidth versus GaAs capping layer thickness compared against prior published data. Linewidth scales down to 0.13 nm at 10 nm thickness, up to 5 times narrower than previous extrapolations.
items.abstract: Epitaxial quantum dots (QDs) are widely recognised as one of the best quantum light sources, given their good stability, brightness, quantum efficiency and coherence. To reach such properties, QDs are protected from potentially detrimental surface states by a relatively thick capping layer, typically exceeding 50nm. This prevents the implementation of near-field effects, like plasmonic-based ones, that can dramatically increase the light-matter interaction, since the control of the spontaneous emission dynamics and directionality of the emission can only occur if the emitter is in close proximity (typically tens of nanometers or less) from the metallic structures. In this work, we report the growth and optical characterisation of InAs/GaAs QDs with GaAs capping layer thickness of 10nm, 20nm, and a more standard 95nm. Remarkably, we observe emission linewidths up to 5 times smaller than previously reported, with unperturbed excitonic lifetimes. These results demonstrate that the epitaxial QD's high optical quality can be maintained even when the emitters are at reduced distances from the surface, opening the path for the exploration of near-field light-matter interactions with coherent and stable emitters, suitable for quantum technology applications.

items.title: Quantum synchronization in atom-cavity coupled systems
items.authors: Katha Haldar, Anushree Dey, Saikat Ghosh, Bimalendu Deb
items.matched: Coherent control of macroscopic quantum states in a single-Cooper-pair box
items.result: Atom-mediated coupling induces limit cycles in undriven cavity modes and out-of-phase quantum synchronization when driven weakly, with Wehrl mutual information showing strict anti-correlation with field synchronization.
items.question: Can atom-mediated coupling between two driven cavity modes induce a two-mode quantum limit cycle and generate phase-locked field dynamics?
items.limits: Requires strong-coupling cavity QED regime with cavity decay rates κ₁, κ₂ ≪g₁, g₂, Ω_i, and large excited-state detuning |Δ_d| ≫g_i, Ω, Γ_d.
items.tools: effective operator adiabatic elimination · SU(2) coherent states over Fock subspaces · generalized two-mode Husimi-Q function · Wehrl mutual information · quantum trajectory method
items.caption: Husimi-Q distribution Q_field(θ,φ), synchronization measure S_field(φ), and single-mode Wigner distributions W_i(x_i,p_i) for weak cavity drives Ω₁=Ω₂=0.005Γ_d, showing phase localization and out-of-phase synchronization across the two cavity modes.
items.abstract: We consider a cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED) setup where an ensemble of spin-1 atoms driven by a classical field interacts with two driven cavity field modes. We show that the two sub-systems - the atoms and the two-mode cavity field, exhibit limit-cycle or quantum synchronization depending on the cavity drive strengths and other system parameters. In order to visualize the limit cycle and synchronization in the field, we introduce generalized two-mode field Husimi-Q function using SU(2) coherent states. For atomic spin states, we make use of spin-1 Husimi-Q function to visualize the same. We further corroborate the occurrence of field synchronization and limit cycle by analyzing U(1) symmetry breaking, Wigner quasi-probability distribution, coherence properties of reduced field density matrix. Our results reveal intriguing interplay between the limit-cycle and quantum synchronization behavior, highlighting emergent quantum phenomena in driven dissipative interacting quantum systems. Additionally, we calculate Wehrl mutual information between the two modes and find that the field synchronization and Wehrl mutual information are mutually exclusive. Our study would be important to extract quantum advantages in quantum metrology using coupled atom-cavity systems.

items.title: Strongly coupled ultracompressed self-cavity plasmon polaritons at millikelvin temperatures
items.authors: Luojia Zhang, Andrew T. Pierce, Xuepeng Wang, Simon Reinhardt, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Kin Fai Mak, Jie Shan, Debanjan Chowdhury, Valla Fatemi
items.matched: Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…
items.result: Realized kinetic inductance broadside cavities with ∼10⁷ volume compression and slow plasmons (v_p≈c/100), observing underdamped cavity-plasmon polaritons down to 0.04 THz and avoided crossings with ∼15ps graphene plasmon lifetime.
items.question: Can sub-terahertz cavity-matter polaritonic modes in van der Waals heterostructures be probed with high frequency resolution at millikelvin temperatures?
items.prior: was 30 to 40 times lower plasmon lifetime using normal metal counter-plates
items.limits: Measurements restricted to T_base≈10mK under frequency limit 4Δ/h≈190GHz set by Al Josephson junction gap; plasmon lifetime appears limited by cavity length via edge scattering.
items.tools: Josephson junction sub-THz spectrometer · NbN/hBN/graphene heterostructures · dilution refrigerator (T_base≈10mK)
items.caption: Real input impedance plotted against carrier density and frequency up to 200 GHz for an NbN/graphene/NbN trilayer cavity. Avoided crossings between the nondispersing cavity mode at ∼170GHz and dispersing graphene plasmon mode demonstrate strong light-matter coupling.
items.abstract: Van der Waals heterostructures exhibit self-cavity resonances from sub-terahertz to terahertz frequencies and thus offer an attractive route toward realizing cavity-modified phases of matter. Spectroscopy of such systems calls for high frequency resolution at millikelvin temperatures, which is extremely challenging with existing methods. Here we demonstrate a new platform for realizing and probing such systems. Superconducting layers define self-cavity structures with electromagnetic volume compression of order 10⁷. With an integrated graphene layer, we observe underdamped cavity plasmon polaritons at frequencies as low as 0.04 THz and which exhibit avoided crossings with cavity modes. To measure such spectra, we deploy a millikelvin-compatible sub-THz spectrometer based on a superconducting circuit. This work paves the way for simultaneous spectroscopy and transport measurements of cavity-matter hybrid systems at millikelvin temperatures.

items.title: Nutational Spin Pumping and Dissipation
items.authors: Hans Gløckner Giil, Arne Brataas
items.matched: materials-limited loss: two-level systems, interfaces, valley splitting
items.result: Introduced dissipative nutational damping term α_ηηm×(m×ddotm) to inertial LLG theory. It generates a dc nutational spin-pumping current J_(s,z)^nsp∝ω² and broadens the nutational linewidth to α+α_η while leaving FMR linewidth at α.
items.question: Does a novel form of nutational damping and spin pumping emerge in the ultrafast THz magnetization dynamics regime?
items.limits: Linearized small-angle precession regime, norm-preserving magnetization, lowest evanescent FM modes.
items.tools: inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation · scattering matrix formulation beyond frozen-in approximation · linear response susceptibility analysis
items.caption: Schematic of spin pumping into an adjacent normal metal, showing linear conventional spin current J_(s,z)^sp∝ω alongside the quadratic nutational spin current J_(s,z)^nsp∝ω².
items.abstract: At terahertz drive frequencies, magnetization dynamics enter an inertial regime beyond the scope of standard Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) theory. We reveal a nutational damping torque comprising a bulk term and an interfacial contribution that describes spin emission into adjacent metals. The interfacial term generates nutational spin pumping: a dc spin current that scales quadratically with the drive frequency. Using a scattering approach, we relate this effect to microscopic material parameters and predict pronounced enhancements in ultrathin films and low-Fermi-energy conductors. Nutational spin pumping can be detected directly via the inverse spin Hall effect or indirectly via thickness-dependent renormalization of nutational damping.

items.title: Quantum Key Distribution with Entanglement-Swapped Photons from a Quantum Emitter
items.authors: Michele B. Rota, Francesco Basso Basset, Alessandro Laneve, Francesco Salusti, Nicolas Claro-Rodriguez, Giuseppe Ronco, Mattia Beccaceci, Tobias M. Krieger, Quirin Buchinger, Saimon F. Covre da Silva, Sandra Stroj, Mariia Gumberidze, Vladyslav Usenko, Sven Höfling, Tobias Huber-Loyola, Mario A. Usuga Castaneda, Armando Rastelli, Klaus D. Jöns, Rinaldo Trotta
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Secret key distribution implemented using entanglement-swapped photons from a GaAs quantum dot, yielding an estimated secure key rate of 1×10⁻³bit at optimal 30ps BSM temporal post-selection.
items.question: Can correlated photons generated from a deterministic quantum emitter and distributed via all-photonic entanglement swapping support secure quantum key distribution?
items.limits: Asymptotic limit. Employs single-emitter temporal multiplexing rather than independent remote quantum dots; requires high temporal filtering (30ps) to overcome distinguishability limits.
items.tools: strain-tuned GaAs/AlGaAs quantum dot in circular Bragg resonator · resonant two-photon excitation (biexciton-exciton cascade) · linear optics Bell state measurement (BSM) · asymmetric source-independent Ekert QKD protocol · high-resolution temporal post-selection
items.caption: Quantum bit error rate (QBER) and Bell parameter S plotted against BSM coincidence time window. Shows the trade-off where narrower time windows reduce error and push S above the classical limit of 2.
items.abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a fundamental functionality of quantum networks. Extending its range requires quantum repeaters, a technology still under development and not yet demonstrated in combination with quantum cryptographic protocols. Here, we address the elementary operation of a viable quantum repeater scheme by evaluating whether correlated photons distributed via entanglement swapping can support secret key distribution. We employ a state-of-the-art deterministic photon source based on a strain-tuned GaAs quantum dot embedded in a photonic cavity and implement a source-independent QKD protocol between two nodes using entanglement-swapped photons. We benchmark the system and present how high-resolution temporal post-selection can enable secure key exchange, with further rate improvements expected through realistic device and protocol optimizations. Due to its compatibility with a wide range of quantum memory platforms, our approach represents a significant step towards long-distance quantum-safe communication.

items.title: Gap-Protected Heisenberg-Limited Squeezing with Locally Interacting Multi-Level Spins
items.authors: Sakshi Bahamnia, Sagar Chaudhary, Arman Duha, Thomas Bilitewski
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Adding local su(D) exchange interactions restores Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing ξ² ∝1/N in multi-level spin arrays across spatial dimensions d=1,2,3 for any power-law interaction exponent α.
items.question: Can gap protection enable Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing in multi-level qudit arrays with finite-range interactions?
items.prior: Without protection, squeezing scales as ξ²_min ∝N^(-ν) with ν≈1 only for αlesssimd/2, degrading to ν≈1/2 at α=d and νlesssim0.05 for αgtrsim3d/2.
items.limits: Valid during early-time exponential growth regime before depletion (n_(i,±1) ≪1). Assumes periodic boundary conditions and gap-protection strength above critical threshold χgtrsimχ_c(L).
items.tools: Bogoliubov spin-wave theory · Discrete truncated Wigner approximation (dTWA) · SU(3) Casimir gap protection · Schwinger boson mapping
items.caption: Minimal spin squeezing parameter ξ²_min and scaling exponent ν versus gap protection strength χ, showing the transition to Heisenberg scaling ξ²_min ∝1/N in 1D, 2D, and 3D arrays.
items.abstract: We demonstrate a general mechanism to generate scalable, metrologically useful entanglement in the form of generalized spin squeezing in multi-level (qudit) spin systems with power-law interactions. We demonstrate this for spin-changing dynamics, extending the physics of spin-nematic squeezing known from spinor BECs to spatially extended lattice geometries. In the absence of all-to-all connectivity, the dynamics generally suffers from leakage into non-collective finite-momentum modes, destroying Heisenberg scaling. We show that introducing local su(D) exchange interactions establishes an energy gap that protects the fully symmetric collective manifold, suppressing non-collective excitations, and achieving Heisenberg scaling ξ²∝1/N in one to three dimensions for any power-law exponent. We provide an analytical understanding of the mechanism via the analysis of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, and demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical simulations of the quantum many-body dynamics. Our findings more broadly apply to other spin-squeezing Hamiltonians, and directly generalize to larger internal spin dimensions. Our results provide a practical pathway towards scalable Heisenberg-limited qudit entanglement generation in experimental platforms such as arrays of (polar) molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg atoms realizing multi-level spin systems.

items.authors: Tomohiro Yamazaki
items.matched: Long-distance quantum communication with atomic ensembles and linear optics
items.result: 2D qubit cluster states generated from 5-qudit 1D cluster states using pairwise fusion gates and adaptive single-qudit measurements, achieving fusion success probability 1-1/d without ancilla photons.
items.question: Whether universal quantum computation can be performed using pairwise fusion gates on qudits while maintaining the boosted fusion success probability 1-1/d.
items.prior: Standard linear-optical fusion success probability was 50% without ancillae, or up to 75% requiring Bell state or single-photon ancillae.
items.limits: Loss tolerance saturates at large d because pairwise fusion gates boost fusion probability but require successful single-qudit measurements; loss of photons representing graph vertices neglected in percolation model.
items.tools: subspace ZX calculus · pairwise fusion gates (PFG) · connecting and merging measurements · percolation threshold simulations

items.abstract: In this paper, we propose a linear-optical quantum computation scheme that starts from high-dimensionally entangled qudits but performs quantum computation on qubits defined in their subspaces. This approach enables us to increase the success probability of linear-optical fusions from 50% to 1-1/d for qudits of dimension d without relying on existing approaches using ancilla photons and quantum codes. In particular, we show that a 2D cluster state of qubits can be generated from 5-qudit 1D cluster states using pairwise fusion gates while preserving their boosted success probability. We numerically demonstrate that this approach can improve the loss tolerance of a percolation-based scheme while keeping the photon number per resource state constant.

items.title: Single-photon addition to multimode quantum fields at telecom wavelengths using lithium niobate and its doped variants
items.authors: Naveen V, Nicolas Treps, Raghavan G, Valentina Parigi, Srinivasan K
items.matched: cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks
items.result: Collinear type-II PDC enables mode-selective single-photon addition in 5% MgO:LN at 1556nm for temperatures between 0^∘C and 15^∘C (K=1.003 at 15^∘C), whereas noncollinear type-I PDC enables single-photon addition with Schmidt number K=1.00002 in 2% ZnO:LN.
items.question: Which phase-matching and group-velocity matching conditions allow spectro-temporal single-photon addition and mode-selective addition to multimode quantum fields at telecom wavelengths using lithium niobate and its doped variants?
items.prior: Mode-selective addition was known to be impossible in congruently grown bulk lithium niobate at room temperature because phase-matching and group-velocity matching cannot coincide.
items.limits: Numerical simulations based on bulk crystal Sellmeier fits; requires cryogenic/sub-ambient cooling down to 0^∘C to 15^∘C for type-II mode selectivity.
items.tools: Collinear type-II parametric down-conversion · Noncollinear type-I parametric down-conversion · Joint spectral amplitude Schmidt decomposition · Sellmeier equations for LN, MgO:LN, and ZnO:LN
items.caption: Phase-matching and group-velocity matching angles versus pump wavelength in 5% MgO:LN at 15^∘C. The intersection at λ= 778.32nm indicates simultaneous phase-matching and group-velocity matching for mode-selective photon addition at 1556nm.
items.abstract: Multimode spectro-temporal non-Gaussian quantum states of light play a crucial role in continuous-variable quantum information processing. In particular, the non-Gaussian quantum states generated through a single-photon addition (SPA) to multimode quantum fields at telecommunication wavelengths constitute a useful resource for quantum technologies. We present a detailed theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of single-photon addition (SPA) and mode-selective single-photon addition (MSSPA) to a multimode quantum field at telecommunication wavelengths. The analysis is performed for congruently grown lithium niobate (LN), 5% MgO-doped lithium niobate (MgO:LN) and various concentrations of ZnO-doped lithium niobate (ZnO:LN) bulk crystals. We investigate MSSPA using type-II parametric down-conversion (PDC) and SPA using the type-I PDC processes. We further present spectro-temporal mode-selective SPA at the telecom wavelength using 5% MgO:LN for temperatures ranging from 0^∘ C to 15^∘ C. In addition, we perform simulations to investigate SPA based on the noncollinear type-I PDC configuration. These theoretical results identify optimal experimental conditions and phase-matching parameters to achieve SPA and mode-selective SPA for LN-based crystals, providing a potential platform for non-Gaussian quantum state engineering at telecommunication wavelengths, mainly at 1550 nm.

items.title: Design Automation for Gray-Code Quantum Read-Only Memory
items.authors: Hao-Yu Lu, Yu-Ting Kao, Yeong-Jar Chang, Chao-Hung Wang, Darsen D. Lu
items.matched: trapped-ion gates, shuttling and QCCD architectures
items.result: Gray-code quantum read-only memory (GQROM) and its electronic design automation (EDA) flow minimize state transition complexity by restricting consecutive address differences to a single bit.
items.question: How to design an automated, low-overhead quantum read-only memory architecture for loading classical data into quantum circuits?
items.limits: Validated in simulation via Qiskit platform.
items.tools: Gray code encoding · Electronic design automation (EDA) flow · Qiskit platform · Quantum read-only memory (QROM)
items.abstract: We propose a programmable quantum read-only memory based on Gray code encoding, termed GQROM, designed to efficiently load classical data into quantum circuits. This architecture mitigates critical bottlenecks in near-term quantum computing by reducing initialization overhead and gate-induced errors. By utilizing Gray code, in which consecutive addresses differ by only a single bit, GQROM minimizes state transition complexity. We demonstrate the architecture's flexibility in accessing targeted data through initial-state modification. The entire design, including a systematic EDA flow, was implemented and validated on the Qiskit platform, confirming its practical feasibility. These results underscore GQROM's potential as a scalable and hardware-friendly solution for efficient state preparation in quantum circuits.

items.title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins
items.authors: Matteo Mezzadri, Silvia Macedonio, Luca Lepori, Emilio Macaluso, Francesco Albarelli, Richard E. P. Winpenny, Alessandro Chiesa, Stefano Carretta1
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Two-level error-correcting encoding combines embedded dephasing correction in S-mathscrs molecular spin dimers with an outer multi-qubit code, bypassing the loss of transferred coherence in anharmonic qudits.
items.question: How can fault-tolerant quantum error correction handle both diagonal dephasing and off-diagonal relaxation errors in single-molecule spin architectures?
items.limits: Simulated under Markovian secular spin-bath dynamics at B_z=0.35 T; assumes ideal syndrome measurement and two-qubit gates on the outer code; inter-molecule entanglement mechanisms not implemented.
items.tools: Redfield master equation · Knill–Laflamme conditions · Pauli twirling approximation · Steane [[7,1,3]] code · Star-shaped multi-spin clusters
items.caption: Entanglement infidelity P_err of planar logical rotations versus dephasing time T₂ for embedded S=3/2 and S=7/2 units at different relaxation times T₁, compared against bare spin-1/2 qubits.
items.abstract: We propose multi-spin molecules as a viable architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. To this aim, we introduce a correction protocol handling both diagonal and off-diagonal errors, typically associated with dephasing and relaxation. The scheme is based on a hybrid encoding which combines dephasing-tolerant units suppressing the leading pure dephasing error into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. Our proposal leverages peculiar properties of molecular spins, i.e. the strong hierarchy between different errors and the possibility to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Moreover, it addresses the important issue of the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which hampers their correction at the single spin level. Thanks to the huge suppression of dephasing by the first-level code, we numerically demonstrate the potential performance of this strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.

items.title: Two-body control of noiseless subsystems with mixed SU(3) representations lifts teleportation above the classical fidelity limit
items.authors: Otavio A. D. Molitor, Sergii Strelchuk, Michał Studziński
items.matched: Long-distance quantum communication with atomic ensembles and linear optics
items.result: Adjacent exchanges and one singlet-projector interaction between fundamental and dual qutrits generate all special unitary gates independently across all noiseless subsystems for any r,s≥1. For four-qutrit encoded teleportation under correlated Weyl noise, logical fidelity exceeds the classical bound 1/2 while unencoded teleportation is entanglement breaking.
items.question: Can two-body symmetry-preserving interactions provide independent logical control across a mixed register of fundamental and dual qutrits without extra initialized ancillas?
items.prior: Fundamental-qutrit registers required three-body interactions for semi-universality, or two-body interactions using six ancillas (Hulse et al. 2021).
items.limits: Pure and mixed tensor SU(3) collective noise only; gate sequence synthesis algorithm not provided; requires retaining trials where all 4 (or 5) qutrits arrive; diamond-norm perturbation bounds assume input-independent survival probabilities.
items.tools: walled Brauer algebra · Lie-algebra control theory · mixed Schur-Weyl duality · correlated Weyl noise channel model · numerical pulse sequence optimization
items.caption: Teleportation fidelity plotted against transmission noise parameter. Identifies the noise interval where unencoded teleportation drops below the entanglement-breaking threshold while encoded teleportation stays above the classical fidelity bound of 1/2.
items.abstract: Collective noise can leave degrees of freedom unaffected, allowing them to store quantum information. Processing this information also requires physically available logical gates. We consider r fundamental qutrits transforming under U∈SU(3) and s dual qutrits transforming under its complex conjugate overlineU, with collective action R_(r,s)(U)=U^(⊗r)⊗overlineU^(⊗s). Using the image of the walled Brauer algebra and Lie-algebra arguments, we show that adjacent exchanges within each qutrit type and one singlet-projector interaction between the two types generate any independently chosen family of special unitary gates on the noiseless subsystems by a finite pulse sequence, for every r,s≥1. This establishes semi-universality of this system. We illustrate the result with a numerically optimised sequence of 24 pulses for three fundamental qutrits and one dual qutrit. We then use the encoding and available logical corrections for qutrit teleportation under correlated Weyl noise. Under explicit assumptions on channel composition and which trials are retained, and allowing for baseline implementation errors, we identify noise ranges in which encoded teleportation exceeds the classical fidelity bound of 1/2, while the unencoded teleportation channel is entanglement breaking. We analyse fidelity on accepted trials separately from the transmission costs of the additional physical qutrits.

items.title: Chiral Vacuum Engineering of Quantum Hall Matter
items.authors: Kiran M. Kulkarni, Andrey Baydin, Motoaki Bamba, Junichiro Kono, Ceren B. Dag, Vasil Rokaj
items.matched: Quantum information with Rydberg atoms
items.result: Coupling a 2DEG to a chiral cavity isolates resonant from antiresonant vacuum interactions, yielding a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity ρ_xy^((s)) = h/(νe²) - s m^*γ² D / (n_2D e² ω_cav²) and an unsqueezed or two-mode squeezed ground state for co- or counter-rotating modes.
items.question: How does a circularly polarized, time-reversal-symmetry-breaking chiral cavity vacuum modify the polariton spectrum, ground state, and DC magnetotransport of a two-dimensional electron gas?
items.prior: In achiral or linearly polarized cavities, Hall resistivity is immune to polariton broadening and light-matter coupling at zero temperature, satisfying ρ_xy^ach = h/(νe²).
items.limits: Spatially uniform cavity field (Kohn's theorem center-of-mass coupling), leading order in polariton broadening γ, zero temperature.
items.tools: Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian · Hopfield-Bogoliubov diagonalization · SU(2) and SU(1,1) algebraic symmetries · Drude-type DC transport inversion
items.caption: Polariton eigenspectra, longitudinal resistivity, and Hall resistivity versus magnetic field B for counter-rotating (CRI) and co-rotating (CRA) chiral cavity modes, showing mode crossing versus anticrossing and handedness-dependent Hall corrections.
items.abstract: We reveal that a chiral cavity distinguishes the resonant and antiresonant interactions between a two-dimensional electron gas and the cavity vacuum. For co-rotating helicities, the modes anticross, exhibiting vacuum Rabi splitting, and retain a bare vacuum ground state. For counter-rotating helicities, the modes cross, acquiring vacuum-mediated energy shifts and a two-mode squeezed ground state. We trace the origin of these observations to the SU(2) and SU(1,1) symmetries of the respective Hamiltonians and present their spectroscopic signatures in chiral photonic crystal cavities. We further predict that cavity chirality produces a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity at finite polariton broadening, while such a correction is not present in an achiral cavity. For the longitudinal resistivity, we find an asymmetric response of the Shubnikov--de Haas oscillations for the different helicities. Finally, we present an experimentally accessible route for detecting the squeezed ground state through current fluctuations. Parameters based on a recently demonstrated terahertz chiral cavity place these effects within experimental reach.

items.title: Low-Overhead Quantum Error Correction with Boundary-Connected Planar Modules
items.authors: Oscar Higgott, Hasan Sayginel, Francisco J. H. Heras, Zhiyang He, Tomas Jochym-O'Connor, Andrew W. Senior, Lei M. Zhang, Thomas Edlich, James S. Spencer, Matt McEwen, Craig Gidney, Johannes Bausch, Pushmeet Kohli, Hartmut Neven
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Constructing modular hyperbolic surface and color codes by wiring static boundary connections between Euclidean planar modules reduces physical qubit overhead by ≥10× compared to planar surface codes under circuit-level noise. Larger modular codes reach encoding rate k/n=1/16 with distance d≥22, exceeding the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle code.
items.question: Can low-overhead quantum error-correcting codes be implemented using mostly nearest-neighbor connectivity on flat planar modules connected only via sparse boundary links?
items.prior: Planar surface codes require high physical qubit overhead; standard high-rate LDPC codes like the [[288,12,18]] bivariate bicycle code require non-planar 2D routing across all qubits.
items.limits: Circuit-level numerical simulations, assumes static inter-module links restricted to module boundaries and standard depolarizing noise models.
items.tools: Semi-hyperbolic surface and color codes · Boundary-connected Euclidean planar modules · Circuit-level noise simulations · Neural network and minimum-weight perfect matching decoders · Fault-tolerant walking circuits
items.abstract: Realizing practical quantum computers requires quantum error correction, but the most widely implemented approach, the planar surface code, demands a substantial physical qubit overhead. Here, we demonstrate that partitioning quantum processors into manageable, flat modules with non-local inter-module connections provides a natural solution. By wiring sparse, static boundary connections between Euclidean planar modules, we construct modular hyperbolic surface and color codes, based on new families of semi-hyperbolic codes. Using modular syndrome extraction circuits and efficient neural network and matching decoders, our circuit-level simulations show that this modular memory design can reduce the physical qubit overhead by tenfold or more compared to the surface code, even under elevated inter-module seam error rates. Projecting to larger system sizes, we find modular codes with encoding rate k/n=1/16 and distance d≥22, exceeding both the rate and distance of the [[288,12,18]] two-gross bivariate bicycle code while using mostly nearest-neighbor gates within planar modules, and implying an over 30× overhead reduction relative to surface codes. We develop fault-tolerant walking circuits for implementing logic via code automorphisms, which we co-design with low-weight, highly symmetrical logical bases and a modular extractor system that is ≈4.5× smaller than the code itself. Combining these methods, our modular memory can be used as dense storage in a universal fault-tolerant architecture, unlocking the efficiency of high-rate codes without sacrificing the fabrication advantages of planar modules.

Larger modular codes reach encoding rate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>/</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>/</mi><mn>16</mn></mrow></math> with distance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>22</mn></mrow></math>, exceeding the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" form="prefix" stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>288,12,18</mn><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" form="postfix" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></math> bivariate bicycle code.

items.title: SpiderCSS: Scalable Fault-Tolerant CSS State Preparation
items.authors: Boldizsár Poór, Andrey Boris Khesin, Sarah Meng Li, Benjamin Rodatz, John van de Wetering, Richie Yeung
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Constructs fault-tolerant CSS state preparation circuits via polynomial-time ZX-calculus rewrites, lowering logical error rate by an average of 33.7%, raising acceptance rate by 9.5%, and cutting CNOT count by up to 53.8% across codes up to distance 15.
items.question: How can fault-tolerant CSS state preparation circuits be synthesized scalably with reduced circuit depth and qubit overhead?
items.prior: Flag at Origin (FaO) modular flagged gadgets (Khesin et al. 2024), limited by offline gadget generation and large depth.
items.limits: Restricted to CSS states and CSS noise (standard unidealization rules fail for non-CSS stabilizer codes); evaluated under circuit-level depolarizing noise (p=10⁻³ and p=10⁻⁴); post-selection discards states with ≥d/2 syndrome faults.
items.tools: ZX-calculus · Fault Tolerance by Construction framework · SpiderCat FT CAT-state synthesis · Stim Monte Carlo simulations · CP-SAT exact scheduler
items.caption: Scatter plots of percentage improvements of SpiderCSS over the FaO baseline for CSS states up to distance 15. The left panel shows logical error rate reduction vs. acceptance rate increase; the right panel shows circuit depth reduction vs. active qubit count reduction under footprint- and depth-optimizing reuse.
items.abstract: Fault-tolerant preparation of logical states is a critical primitive for the realization of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. This paper introduces SpiderCSS, a scalable compilation pipeline that generates highly-optimized, fault-tolerant state preparation circuits for arbitrary Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes. Starting from an idealized specification of a CSS state, we use the ZX-calculus and fault-equivalent rewrites to construct a diagram that prepares the given state while preserving the fault tolerance of the initial ideal ZX-diagram. From this diagram, SpiderCSS constructs a fault-tolerant CSS-state preparation circuit using a modular construction that is CNOT-minimal both within each component and also in the way these components are connected together. By only using fault-equivalent rewrites, the final circuit is provably fault-tolerant without needing expensive verification. Monte Carlo simulations across a variety of CSS codes up to distance 15 show that SpiderCSS scales efficiently and constructs circuits with substantially reduced depth and qubit footprint compared to existing scalable and heuristic methods, while simultaneously achieving an average decrease of 33.7% in logical error rate and an increase of 9.5% in acceptance rate.

items.title: Fault-tolerant and fully addressable unitary logical gates via round-robin sparsification
items.authors: Kaavya Sahay, Cody Jones
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Round-robin circuits sparsified via stabilizer deformations implement fully addressable, fault-tolerant transversal CZ gates with circuit depth independent of code distance for 2D translationally invariant qLDPC codes. On a 288-qubit gross code (d=12), the addressable tCZ achieves ∼4× lower spacetime overhead and ∼5× lower logical error impact than code surgery.
items.question: How can fully addressable, fault-tolerant, low-depth transversal logical two-qubit Clifford gates be realized on quantum low-density parity check codes without multi-round code surgery?
items.prior: Addressable logical operations on qLDPC codes relied primarily on lattice surgery taking O(d) measurement rounds, or on transversal constructions limited in code distance or stabilizer structure.
items.limits: Restricted to 2D translationally invariant qLDPC codes, evaluated primarily on periodic boundary conditions; complex codes with incomplete disjoint representative sets require either an intermediate stabilizer round to restore full distance d or accept distance reduction to d/2.
items.tools: Round-robin sparsification · Stabilizer deformations · Cylinder trick (sliding cylinder) · Stim/Stimflow numerical simulations
items.caption: Logical error rate versus physical error rate for the 288-qubit d=12 gross code comparing an addressable transversal CZ against code surgery (XX measurement) and quantum memory baselines, showing fault-tolerant error suppression.
items.abstract: For quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes, the ability to manipulate individual logical units of information, i.e. the use of addressable gates, enables maximal utility of their efficient encoding. We introduce explicit low-depth unitary circuits that realize fully addressable and fault-tolerant two-qubit Clifford gates for a subset of two-dimensional translationally invariant qLDPC codes. Our transversal unitaries are created by applying a geometrically structured sparsification procedure to round-robin circuits. We verify the general applicability of our protocol by proposing and numerically simulating a range of addressable CZs between toric, cyclic hypergraph-product, color, gross, and directional codes, demonstrating fault-tolerant memory-like logical error rate scaling.
