items.title: Single-Shot Error Correction at Optimal Spacetime Cost
items.authors: Kishor Bharti, Tobias Haug, Derek Khu, Andrew Tanggara
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Encoded quantum memory achieves optimal spacetime cost C = O(S(K + log(S/ε))) using an explicit noisy syndrome extraction circuit and O(N) classical decoding work per cycle. Relative spacetime overhead C/(KS) = O(1 + log(S/ε)/K) is constant for K = Ω(log(S/ε)).
items.question: Can the optimal spacetime cost Ω(S(K+log(S/ε))) for storing K logical qubits for S steps with error at most ε be attained using realistic, noisy quantum error correction circuits and efficient decoding?
items.prior: Lower bound Ω(S(K+log(S/ε))) was matched only under idealized error correction (Bharti et al. 2024); independent surface code patches require O(KSlog²(KS/ε)).
items.limits: Requires long-range qubit connectivity, fast and reliable parallel classical processing, error strength below threshold p < p_*, and input/output remaining encoded in the code blocks.
items.tools: quantum Tanner codes · single-shot decoding · local-stochastic circuit noise model · Knill-Laflamme conditions for coherent errors
items.caption: Schematic of optimal memory protocol: single-round check measurements and fixed-iteration decoding maintain residual error below the correctable threshold, sharing the O(log(S/ε)) reliability overhead across K logical qubits over S cycles.
items.abstract: Recent work established that, for independent erasures, storing K logical qubits for S time steps with error at most ε requires a spacetime cost of Ω(S(K+log(S/ε))). A matching construction was also given, but assumes ideal error correction. Here we show that the same scaling can be achieved with an explicit noisy error-correction circuit and efficient decoding, counting all state-preparation, gate, measurement, and wait locations, provided that the hardware supports long-range qubit connectivity and fast, reliable classical processing. Thus, reliability adds only a logarithmic overhead shared by all stored qubits. The construction works for sufficiently weak but otherwise general circuit noise, including faults during syndrome extraction and correlated faults, and for independent erasures it matches the best known lower bound up to constant factors. We attain this scaling using quantum Tanner codes, with each memory step consisting of one round of syndrome extraction followed by a fixed number of parallel classical decoder steps that reduce the residual error enough to keep later faults correctable, regardless of memory size, storage time, or target accuracy. Together, this gives exponentially small failure probability per step while keeping the cost of each memory step linear in the code size. The same analysis also extends to certain constant-depth logical Clifford operations.

items.title: Fault tolerance of quantum circuits with tensor networks and symplectic geometry
items.authors: Soham Ghosh, Holger Boche, Andrew Tanggara
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Establishes operator-algebraic necessary and sufficient conditions for quantum circuit fault tolerance under general noise, yielding closed-form detection and logical-effect matrices for stabilizer circuits and linear-programming upper bounds on circuit distance.
items.question: How can fault tolerance and circuit distance be certified and bounded algebraically across general and stabilizer quantum circuits under arbitrary noise models?
items.limits: Non-adaptive stabilizer circuits for closed-form matrices; independent and identically distributed depolarizing noise for weight-enumerator pseudothreshold bounds.
items.tools: Quantum-comb formalism · Semidefinite programming (SDP) · Linear programming (LP) · Symplectic geometry · MacWilliams identities
items.caption: A two-round adaptive quantum circuit interacting with causally correlated noise via instrument modules, classical measurement records, and noise memory systems before a final noiseless recovery operation.
items.abstract: We develop an operator-algebraic framework for analyzing fault tolerance in quantum circuits and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for fault tolerance under any given noise model. For prescribed circuit families and noise models, we derive a semidefinite program (SDP) based test whose infeasibility certifies that there does not exist any recovery map restoring its intended operation. For non-adaptive stabilizer circuits, analyzing the stabilizer symmetries of its components with symplectic geometry, we obtain closed-form detection and logical-effect matrices that characterize circuit distance algebraically. Applied to a finite Hastings--Haah honeycomb Floquet-code circuit, these matrices certify the dynamical encoding of two logical qubits and distance four under Pauli noise including measurement errors. Using these matrices, we then derive MacWilliams identities for circuit weight enumerators and obtain linear-programming (LP) upper bounds on circuit distance. Output-code constraints give additional Singleton-like bounds. Under independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) depolarizing noise, the weight enumerators determine decoder failure probabilities and yield upper bounds on finite-circuit pseudothresholds. Finally, we derive LP distance bounds for families of flag syndrome-extraction circuits specified by their CNOT orderings, by incorporating the t-flag criterion as additional linear constraints to the distance-bounding LP. An analytical CSS Hamming-code benchmark yields a tight distance-three bound attained by the Chao--Reichardt one-flag construction.

items.title: High-Rate Quantum Codes with Proven Distance and Low-Weight Measurements
items.authors: Kishor Bharti, Tobias Haug, Runzhou Tao, Kevin Ye
items.matched: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
items.result: Proves dressed distance is D=2^L for any L-dimensional rectangular subsystem code with even side lengths q_i ≥4, data qubits N=∏_i q_i, and logical qubits K=∏_i (q_i-2), with max gauge measurement weight w=max_i q_i.
items.question: How many logical qubits can a finite quantum memory protect under low-weight gauge measurements on rectangular coordinate grids?
items.prior: Uniform side-four and side-six subsystem many-hypercube codes (Nakai and Goto), plus standard subsystem products like SHYPS(6) which achieves [[3969,36,3249,32]] with rate 0.91% vs 13.17% (6⁵ line-gauge code) at distance 32.
items.limits: Static code distance; does not evaluate fault-tolerant circuit distance, noise thresholds, decoder performance, or geometric locality constraints.
items.tools: subsystem codes · binary symplectic formalism · quotient-space distance proof · Lean 4 interactive theorem prover
items.caption: Protected encoding rate K/N plotted against maximum gauge measurement weight w for code distances D=16, 32, 64 under a cap of at most 10,000 data qubits.
items.abstract: We study a family of quantum subsystem codes defined on rectangular coordinate grids of any dimension, with even side lengths of at least four. The directly measured operators act along coordinate lines. For every member of the family, we derive the number of protected logical qubits and prove its dressed distance without a numerical search. To illustrate the resulting design choices, we impose a budget of at most 10,000 data qubits and determine the complete tradeoff between encoding rate and measurement weight within this family at distances 16, 32, and 64. At distance 16, one code protects 4,096 logical qubits among 10,000 data qubits using weight-ten measurements. At distances 32 and 64, codes with 7,776 and 9,216 data qubits protect 1,024 and 256 logical qubits, respectively, using weight-six measurements. We include and explain Lean code snippets throughout the paper to guide readers through the formal verification of our subsystem-code construction and its dressed and bare distances.

items.title: Efficient fidelity simulation of high-rate magic distillation circuits
items.authors: Xiao Xiao, Dominik Hangleiter, J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides, Rohan Mehta, Varun Menon, Mikhail D. Lukin, Michael J. Gullans
items.matched: High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory
items.result: Monte Carlo sampling of syndrome statistics, logical fidelity, and Pauli expectation values for noisy circuits with X, CNOT, and level-3 Clifford-hierarchy diagonal gates runs in O(n³ T) time per sample, with zero scaling dependence on the number of logical qubits.
items.question: How can one efficiently benchmark the fault-tolerant logical performance and syndrome distributions of quantum circuits containing non-Clifford gates under stochastic Pauli noise?
items.prior: Generic exact classical benchmarking incurred a cost exponential in the number of non-Clifford gates or magic measures, or depended separately on the number of logical qubits.
items.limits: Circuit components restricted to X, CNOT, and level-3 diagonal gates (plus Clifford pre/post-processing); syndrome checks must be affected by faults from a constant number of layers; restricted to circuit-level stochastic Pauli noise.
items.tools: Affine-diagonal normal form · Clifford-hierarchy commutator reduction · Monte Carlo fault-path backpropagation · Binary Gaussian elimination syndrome sampling
items.caption: Plots total physical ancilla overhead against logical infidelity of a 9-qubit hypergraph state prepared via a depth-2 CCZ circuit on three [[27,3,3]] tricycle code blocks across syndrome extraction protocols.
items.abstract: Non-Clifford gates are essential for avoiding classical simulability under the Gottesman-Knill theorem. An error-corrected circuit with non-Clifford gates will therefore be an important element for realizing useful fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. However, accurately understanding the fault-tolerant performance of such circuits faces challenges due to the classical hardness of simulating these circuits. We avoid simulating logical measurements and develop exact and efficient classical methods for benchmarking circuits composed of X, CNOT, and diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy, including state and gate teleportation gadgets with feedforward. For circuits with third-level diagonal gates, our benchmarking algorithm efficiently samples syndrome statistics and estimates the output logical fidelity and expectation values of certain Clifford observables, including all Pauli observables. The evaluation of syndrome expectation values also extends to circuits with fourth-level diagonal gates. Our algorithm scales polynomially in the number of physical qubits n and circuit depth T, independent of the number of logical qubits. The benchmarking applications include IQP sampling and magic state preparation/cultivation. We demonstrate the practical utility of our simulation algorithms by using them to optimize high-rate magic state distillation factories based on three copies of a [[27,3,3]] tricycle code.

items.authors: Alison Warman, Nathanan Tantivasadakarn, Sakura Schafer-Nameki

items.result: Constructs an exact, deterministic quantum recovery unitary that moves errors onto ancillas to be projected out for topological surface codes based on the quantum double D(G) of any finite group G.
items.question: How can exact, deterministic error recovery be realized on 2D non-Abelian quantum double surface codes D(G) given non-invertible anyon fusion and non-Abelian stabilizers?

items.caption: Charge transfer circuits that map the irreducible representation error on a direct-lattice edge entering or exiting vertex v onto an ancilla qudit via controlled operations.
items.abstract: We study exact recovery for non-Abelian topological surface codes based on the quantum double D(G) of any finite group G. We determine an orthogonal error basis, that is comprised of group multiplication and irreducible representation operators. Whenever the errors are supported on closed loops on the lattice or dual lattice, there is a redundancy in the basis, due to stabilizers. To remedy this, we introduce a gauge-fixing that results in a complete and orthogonal error basis on the code space. Assuming as input predetermined, neutral correctable error clusters, we construct charge and flux transfer circuits that move the errors onto ancillas that then get projected out. This is an exact and deterministic recovery protocol, applicable to surface codes for any finite, in particular non-Abelian, group G.

items.title: Rate-Optimal Quantum Discrete Simulation Optimization
items.authors: Mingjie Hu, Jian-Qiang Hu
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: Quantum discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap Ω(|X|/T), achieved up to logarithmic factors by the textscQUEST algorithm (O(|X|logT/T)). Convergence rate improves quadratically over budget T compared to classical bound Ω(√|X|/T), with worse scaling in decision count |X|.
items.question: How does quantum computing affect the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting, and can a provably rate-optimal algorithm be designed?
items.prior: Classical discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap lower bound Ω(√|X|/T).
items.limits: Fixed-budget setting with discrete candidate decisions |X|. Continuous observation outputs require finite support discretization onto grid qubits.
items.tools: sequential quantum phase-testing lower bound reduction · quantum Monte Carlo estimation · sequential elimination framework · slow-measurement mechanism · Qiskit numerical simulation
items.caption: Expected optimality gap as a function of simulation budget T under Bernoulli outcomes with |X|=20. Compares the faster decay of the quantum textscQUEST algorithm against the classical textscMC-EST baseline.
items.abstract: Quantum computing has developed rapidly in recent years and has shown potential advantages over classical computing in various domains. In this paper, we study whether quantum computing can accelerate the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting. We first formulate the quantum discrete simulation optimization problem by defining the quantum simulation oracle, the algorithmic performance measure, and the corresponding optimality guarantee. Based on this formulation, we establish a minimax lower bound on the expected optimality gap for any quantum algorithm. The lower bound analysis reduces the discrete simulation optimization problem to a sequential quantum phase-testing problem, and the resulting lower-bound argument may be of independent interest. By comparing the quantum lower bound with its classical counterpart, we show that the optimal convergence rate in the quantum setting exhibits a quadratic improvement in its dependence on the simulation budget, at the cost of a worse dependence on the number of decisions. We then propose the first fixed-budget quantum algorithm, called textscQUEST, for discrete simulation optimization. The algorithm combines a quantum Monte Carlo subroutine with a sequential elimination framework and uses a slow-measurement mechanism to help preserve quantum superposition during the optimization process. We prove that textscQUEST achieves the optimal convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments further show that textscQUEST outperforms its classical counterpart, which provides empirical evidence for the quantum advantage in improving the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization algorithms.

items.title: Breaking the chain: geometry-native state preparation with ASPIRE
items.authors: Fredrik Hasselgren, Matthew L. Sims-Goh
items.matched: Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup
items.result: ASPIRE compiles approximate state-preparation circuits by greedily removing entanglement across hardware-native qubit connectivity. Yields shallower circuits and higher state fidelity than standard sequential staircase circuits, especially for states with long-range entanglement.
items.question: How to compile shallow, hardware-native state preparation circuits for matrix product states without relying on sequential nearest-neighbour gate staircases?
items.prior: Approximate matrix product state preparation relies on layered sequential staircases of nearest-neighbour gates.
items.limits: Heuristic greedy compilation. Evaluated on empirical simulations of Hamiltonian ground states and amplitude-encoded functions under NISQ noise and early fault-tolerant settings.
items.tools: matrix product states · ASPIRE algorithm · entanglement removability scoring · circuit compilation
items.abstract: Loading data into quantum computers is a key bottleneck that threatens end-to-end quantum advantage. Quantum-circuit compilers for structured states like matrix product states (MPS) are a critical enabler to manage this in quantum chemistry, finance, and many-body quantum simulation. Approximate preparation of MPS typically relies on layered sequential staircases of nearest-neighbour gates. We present Adaptive State Preparation by Iterative Removal of Entanglement (ASPIRE), an algorithm that approximately compiles state-preparation circuits by selecting gates based on the state's underlying entanglement geometry and the available connectivity of the target quantum processor. Our protocol scores candidate qubit pairs on the removability of their entanglement and identifies layers of parallelised long-ranged gates that remove the most entanglement. We demonstrate our protocol empirically across a range of settings, illustrating its success for preparing Hamiltonian ground states and multivariate amplitude-encoded functions, and accounting for qubit connectivity, hardware noise, and both NISQ and early fault-tolerant settings. Throughout, ASPIRE typically achieves higher fidelities and shallower circuits than existing methods for states with long-ranged entanglement, even when classical optimisation is accounted for. Our investigation positions ASPIRE as a competitive, resource-frugal state-preparation protocol, with particular promise for applications tolerant to imperfect fidelity such as preparation of guide states for quantum phase estimation.

items.title: Quantum algorithms for orthogonal polynomial transforms
items.authors: Anupam Prakash, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Dylan Herman, Shouvanik Chakrabarti
items.matched: Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…
items.result: Constructs quantum orthogonal polynomial transforms (QOPT) running in O(polylog(N, 1/ε)) time for discrete Charlier, Meixner, and Krawtchouk transforms, and for continuous Laguerre transforms. Achieves an O(Npolylog((N+α+β+1)/ε)) runtime for the discrete Hahn transform.
items.question: Which orthogonal polynomial transforms admit efficient quantum circuit implementations with exponential speedups over classical transforms?
items.prior: Hermite transform runs in poly-logarithmic time (Jain et al. STOC'26); naive Hahn transform is O(N²).
items.limits: Preserves orthogonality approximately up to an energy cutoff; assumes integer parameters for Jacobi-to-Hahn reduction; Wilson, Racah, continuous Hahn, and continuous dual Hahn families not solved.
items.tools: Wei–Norman factorization / Fast-forwarding · Gaussian optical gates on Cartesian grids · SU(2) and SU(1,1) Schwinger representations · 3-term chirp decomposition · Quantum Hankel Transform / FFTLog
items.caption: Hierarchical chart of the Askey scheme of hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials showing the limit transitions between polynomial families and their achieved quantum transform complexities.
items.abstract: A quantum orthogonal polynomial transform (QOPT) is an algorithmic primitive that maps a superposition of standard basis states ∑_k α_k |k⟩ coherently to a basis of normalized univariate polynomials orthogonal with respect to a probability measure μ(x). We provide new discrete and continuous QOPTs for polynomial families in the Askey scheme extending the results for the quantum Hermite transform (Jain et al., STOC'26). Our efficient QOPT algorithms require time O(polylog(N, 1/ε)), where N is the grid size and ε is the error, for the discrete Charlier, Meixner and Krawtchouk transforms and for the integer-order Laguerre transform in the continuous setting. The efficient QOPTs are obtained by uncovering the links between Askey scheme polynomials and Gaussian quantum optical gates and developing a compilation framework for SU(2) and SU(1,1) optical gates on Cartesian grids extending the framework developed by Iyer et al. (arXiv:2602.15180). Further, we reduce the continuous Jacobi transform to the discrete Hahn transform and provide an O (Npolylog((N+α+β+1)/ε))-time Hahn transform, a quadratic speedup over the naive implementation. This is based on a more efficient compilation of the Clebsch--Gordan transform for coupling SU(2) representations with spins (j₁, j₂). Finally, we develop a new framework for Laguerre transforms for all orders ν>0 by fast-forwarding the corresponding radial oscillator using a 3-term chirp decomposition and an efficient algorithm for the Quantum Hankel Transform on a logarithmic grid.

items.title: Unitary complexity in polynomial space
items.authors: William Kretschmer, Ewin Tang
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Every unitary U ∈unitaryPSPACE satisfies either U not∈unitaryP^ALL or U ∈unitaryP^FNEXP. Consequently, existence of quantum commitments implies either no polynomial-time unitary synthesis or BPP ≠NEXP.
items.question: Does the hardness underlying quantum cryptography imply breakthrough classical complexity lower bounds?
items.limits: Garbage-allowed implementations vs. garbage-free implementations coincide up to tensoring with the adjoint.
items.tools: unitary complexity classes (unitaryP, unitaryPSPACE) · unitary synthesis reductions · projective unitary dilations and garbage-state tracking
items.abstract: We show that if quantum commitments exist, then either there is no polynomial-time solution to the unitary synthesis problem, or BPP ≠NEXP. Thus, showing unconditionally that quantum commitments exist would require answering at least one of two longstanding open questions in complexity theory. We prove our main result as a consequence of a more general lemma, which shows that every unitary in unitaryPSPACE either cannot be synthesized efficiently relative to any classical oracle, or can be synthesized efficiently with an oracle for NEXP search problems. Our lemma has other noteworthy consequences, including that certain oracle separations involving unitaryPSPACE would imply breakthrough classical lower bounds such as NC ≠NP. Along the way, we propose new definitions for the unitary complexity classes unitaryP and unitaryPSPACE. Our changes address the biggest conceptual issues with definitions suggested in prior work, and lead to elegant proofs. We study both implementations that erase garbage and implementations that allow it, because we cannot rule out the possibility that the two definitions differ. Nevertheless, we show that both definitions can be viewed as special cases of each other. We also showcase many other ways in which our definitions are robust. For example, we show that unitaryPSPACE has an equivalent characterization as the set of unitary transformations whose entries can be computed to arbitrary precision in polynomial space. Consequently, we deduce that unitaryPSPACE can generically erase garbage, a result that provably fails relative to unitary oracles.

items.title: Exponential lower bounds on the fermionic Gaussian rank of magic states and the bosonic coherent state rank of Fock states
items.authors: Oliver Reardon-Smith
items.matched: Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations
items.result: Fermionic Gaussian rank of |M⟩^(⊗k) is lower bounded by 8/(9(k+1))((27(8+2√7))/256)^k > 8/(9(k+1)) 1.4018^k, with δ-approximate rank bounded by (1-δ²) times this value. Coherent state border rank of n-mode bosonic Fock state |m⟩ is exactly ∏_(j=1)ⁿ(1+m_j).
items.question: What are the exact and approximate rank lower bounds for decomposing magic states into fermionic Gaussian states and Fock states into bosonic coherent states?
items.prior: For fermionic Gaussian rank of |M⟩^(⊗k), only trivial lower bound of 2 was known for k ≥2. For coherent-state border rank of |1⟩^(⊗n), superpolynomial but sub-exponential lower bounds were proved by prior work.
items.limits: Pure states of fixed parity. Fermionic rank bound established for the four-qubit magic state |M⟩= 1/(√2)(|0000⟩+ |1111⟩) and products thereof. Bosonic lower bound applies to coherent states, not the full set of bosonic Gaussian states.
items.tools: matrix rank method · Majorana operator polynomial evaluations · Hankel-type matrix representations · Frobenius and Schatten norms
items.caption: Exact fermionic Gaussian rank of |M⟩^(⊗k) plotted against number of copies k, comparing the asymptotic analytical lower bound, the small-k optimized lower bound, the k=2 bound, and the 2^k upper bound.
items.abstract: Recent algorithms for classical simulation of quantum mechanics have runtime whose superpolynomial component is given by a linear dependence on the number of terms required to write large tensor products of certain "magic" states as superpositions of "free" states (which may be stabilizer states, fermionic Gaussian states or others). Surprisingly little is known about the number of terms in such decompositions, called ranks (e.g. the stabilizer rank, fermionic-Gaussian rank etc.). For complexity theoretic reasons they are expected to grow exponentially in the number of tensor factors but, while exponential upper bounds are known for both the stabilizer and fermionic-Gaussian rank of magic states; the best known lower bounds on the stabiliser rank are quadratic, and no bounds on the fermionic-Gaussian rank are known beyond fixed constants. In this work we prove that any fermionic Gaussian decomposition of |M⟩^(⊗k) consists of Ω(1.4^k) terms. Here |M⟩ is the most standard magic state for fermionic linear optics: the 4 qubit state that may be consumed to implement a swap gate. We also prove essentially matching bounds on the δ-approximate rank of the same state, lower bounding it by the same quantity that bounds the exact rank, multiplied by a factor of 1-δ². Our results on exact fermionic Gaussian rank apply directly to any product of k fixed parity non-Gaussian states, although the same is not true of the approximate rank. Finally, we prove that the coherent state border rank of an n-mode bosonic Fock state with m_j bosons in mode j is exactly ∏_j(1+m_j), answering a conjecture of Ref. [1] and obtain lower bounds on the approximate coherent state rank given by the same quantity multiplied by a function of the fidelity of the approximation, emphasizing the broad applicability of the method we employ.

items.title: Exponential quantum space advantage in random data streams
items.authors: Adam Bouland, Matthew Ding, Siddhartha Jain
items.matched: quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds
items.result: Streaming Yamakawa–Zhandry Code Intersection in random order takes poly(n) qubits versus exp(n^(Ω(1))) classical bits. Streaming Optimal Polynomial Intersection to target value lceiln/2+√dn/8rceil takes O(dlogn) qubits versus Ω(n) classical bits.
items.question: Can quantum algorithms achieve exponential advantage for space complexity in the streaming model when inputs are presented in a uniformly random order?
items.limits: Asymptotic regime with d = ω(logn) and d = o(n/logn) for Optimal Polynomial Intersection; random oracle setting; applies to streaming memory constraints, not general query complexity.
items.tools: density-restoring partitions · convex potential functions on read-once branching programs · decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) · folded Reed–Solomon list-recoverability
items.abstract: We show two unconditional quantum space advantages in the random-order streaming model. First, we show the Yamakawa--Zhandry Code Intersection problem admits exponential quantum advantage in the streaming model when its inputs are streamed in random order. This means quantum computers exhibit exponential space advantage even when simply receiving (x,f(x)) pairs for a uniformly random function f in a uniformly random order. Our lower bound is shown using density-restoring partitions as in the work of Göös, Gur, Jain, and Li (STOC 2025) combined with a convex potential, similar to the work of Raz (J.ACM 2018) on parity learning and its generalization by Garg, Raz, and Tal (STOC 2018). Second, we use our framework to show quantum space advantage for the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem in certain regimes via a streaming version of the Decoded Quantum Interferometry algorithm (Nature 2025; arXiv:2510.10967). In particular, we show that for degree d and n evaluation points, attaining 1/2 + Ω(√d/n) fraction of satisfied OPI constraints via streaming requires Ω(n) classical bits of memory but only O(dlogn) qubits. This yields provable quantum advantage in a "low-rate" regime when the number of evaluation points is much larger than the degree, with a space advantage that can be as large as exponential in certain parameter settings.

items.title: Root-sparsity scaling for Hamiltonian simulation, differential equations and linear-system solvers
items.authors: Dominic W. Berry, Abhishek Rawat, Sophia Simon, Guang Hao Low
items.matched: Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations
items.result: Simulates s-sparse Hamiltonians in O(√sτ+√sτlog(1/ε)+log(1/ε)) queries for τ=η|t|, dissipative linear ODEs in O(barg√sτlog(Cbarg/ε)), and linear systems in O(√sκlog(1/ε)).
items.question: Can quantum algorithms achieve exact square-root sparsity scaling for general sparse Hamiltonian simulation, linear ODEs, and linear system solvers without subpolynomial overheads?
items.prior: Linear-in-s scaling for standard block encodings; previous general √s Hamiltonian simulation required subpolynomial factors from an iterated interaction picture (Low 2019) or conditional norm assumptions (Berry and Childs 2012).
items.limits: Requires sparse oracle access with row/column Euclidean norm bounds η, certified time discretisation for time-dependent cases, and efficient entry decoding circuits for gate implementations.
items.tools: exact entrywise Cayley representation · Cayley transducers · Chebyshev filter · linear combination of Hamiltonian simulations (LCHS) · ordered-rotation factorisation
items.abstract: We give quantum algorithms for Hamiltonian simulation, linear differential equations, and linear systems with square-root dependence on sparsity. For an s-sparse Hermitian matrix with row and column Euclidean norms bounded by η, evolution for time t to error ε uses O(√sτ+√sτlog(1/ε)+log(1/ε)) queries, where τ=η|t|. The same bound holds for time-dependent Hamiltonians with coherent time-indexed sparse access and certified time discretisation. Our construction combines an exact entrywise representation with Cayley transducers. A joint lower bound nearly matches the time, sparsity, and precision dependence, ruling out a uniformly additive bound in √sτ and log(1/ε). For dissipative linear differential equations we obtain O(barg[√s(τ+√τ)+1]log(Cbarg/ε)) queries, where τ is the evolution time multiplied by a norm bound, barg bounds the ratio of combined input and source norms to the final-solution norm, and C is an absolute constant. We sharpen this bound by separating Hamiltonian and dissipative components, and treat general constant generators. Lower bounds capture joint parameter dependence for time-dependent equations and precision hardness for constant positive semidefinite dissipation. For linear systems, a Cayley walk and Chebyshev filter give O(κ√slog(1/ε)) queries when |A|≤1 and |A⁻¹|≤κ, and we give an alternative proof of a matching joint lower bound. We also give gate-efficient implementations of time-independent Hamiltonian simulation and the dissipative ODE solver, including Lipschitz time dependence, retaining the query bounds with polylogarithmic overhead in inverse precision given efficient entry decoding, arithmetic, and required source preparations.

items.title: Symmetry-preserving quantum compilation
items.authors: Maryam Mudassar, Zhi-Yuan Wei, Alexander Schuckert, Michael J. Lawler, Michael J. Gullans, Daniel Gottesman
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Measurement-assisted and LCU Clifford+T compilation synthesizes continuous time evolution while preserving exact continuous symmetries such as SU(2), reducing the required T-count by approximately a factor of five compared to standard symmetry-agnostic compilation for estimating 1D Heisenberg transport exponents.
items.question: How can continuous symmetry-preserving time evolutions be compiled into fault-tolerant discrete gate sets without introducing symmetry-breaking synthesis errors?
items.prior: Standard symmetry-agnostic synthesis (such as gridsynth/Solovay-Kitaev) introduces off-axis transverse errors that break continuous conservation laws and yielded incorrect transport exponents at 54 T gates per two-site Trotter step.
items.limits: Demonstrated for spin-1/2 systems with exact SU(2) symmetry, 1D lattice gauge theories, and fermionic models (Fermi-Hubbard, electronic structure); higher-spin systems remain unexplored.
items.tools: Measurement and feed-forward · Linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · Repeat-until-success (RUS) axial compilation · Jordan–Wigner transformation
items.caption: Transport scaling comparison showing transferred magnetization versus time steps. For matched dynamical transport exponent accuracy (1/z ≈2/3), the symmetry-preserving LCU compilation reduces the cumulative T-count compared to standard synthesis and BRS axial synthesis.
items.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum simulation requires compiling symmetry-preserving time evolutions into discrete gate sets. Standard Clifford+T synthesis can break continuous symmetries even when the target evolution preserves them, causing compiled simulations to lose essential features of the original system. We develop a fault-tolerant compilation framework that preserves SU(2) symmetry exactly. We characterize the number-theoretic obstruction preventing symmetry-preserving unitary Clifford+T circuits from approximating arbitrary SU(2)-symmetric evolutions and circumvent it using measurement and feed-forward. The resulting synthesis confines compilation errors to the symmetry-preserving operator algebra rather than introducing symmetry-breaking perturbations. We demonstrate the algorithm by simulating transport in the one-dimensional Heisenberg model. At a lower matched T-count, for instance, 54 T gates per two-site Trotter step, standard synthesis yields an incorrect transport exponent, whereas our symmetry-preserving compilation reproduces the expected exponent for the same expected T-count. If instead each approach is allocated whatever resources are necessary to estimate this exponent to the same accuracy, our construction reduces the T-count by approximately a factor of five. We further extend the framework to gauge symmetries in lattice gauge theories and to particle-number and spin symmetries in fermionic models relevant to quantum chemistry and the Fermi-Hubbard model. These results show that symmetry-preserving fault-tolerant compilation can qualitatively change the effects of synthesis error while substantially reducing the resources required for quantum simulation.

items.title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins
items.authors: Matteo Mezzadri, Silvia Macedonio, Luca Lepori, Emilio Macaluso, Francesco Albarelli, Richard E. P. Winpenny, Alessandro Chiesa, Stefano Carretta1
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Two-level error-correcting encoding combines embedded dephasing correction in S-mathscrs molecular spin dimers with an outer multi-qubit code, bypassing the loss of transferred coherence in anharmonic qudits.
items.question: How can fault-tolerant quantum error correction handle both diagonal dephasing and off-diagonal relaxation errors in single-molecule spin architectures?
items.limits: Simulated under Markovian secular spin-bath dynamics at B_z=0.35 T; assumes ideal syndrome measurement and two-qubit gates on the outer code; inter-molecule entanglement mechanisms not implemented.
items.tools: Redfield master equation · Knill–Laflamme conditions · Pauli twirling approximation · Steane [[7,1,3]] code · Star-shaped multi-spin clusters
items.caption: Entanglement infidelity P_err of planar logical rotations versus dephasing time T₂ for embedded S=3/2 and S=7/2 units at different relaxation times T₁, compared against bare spin-1/2 qubits.
items.abstract: We propose multi-spin molecules as a viable architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. To this aim, we introduce a correction protocol handling both diagonal and off-diagonal errors, typically associated with dephasing and relaxation. The scheme is based on a hybrid encoding which combines dephasing-tolerant units suppressing the leading pure dephasing error into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. Our proposal leverages peculiar properties of molecular spins, i.e. the strong hierarchy between different errors and the possibility to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Moreover, it addresses the important issue of the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which hampers their correction at the single spin level. Thanks to the huge suppression of dephasing by the first-level code, we numerically demonstrate the potential performance of this strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.

items.title: Quantum simulation of field-tunable spin spectroscopy of the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 on a trapped-ion quantum computer
items.authors: Elias Kokkas, Nora Bauer, Justin Provazza, Mark E. Nowakowski, Kathleen Hamilton, Gilles Buchs, Andrew Sornborger, Travis S. Humble, Ananth Kaushik, Martin Roetteler
items.matched: Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance
items.result: Dynamic spin structure factor and quantum Fisher information density of 36-site Cs₂CoCl₄ chain simulated on 36-qubit quantum processor with 420 two-qubit gates per state. Error-mitigated spectra achieve Pearson correlation and structural similarity > 0.9 against DMRG-CV and Pearson correlation > 0.85 against inelastic neutron scattering.
items.question: How much reliable magnetic spectral information and field evolution can be recovered from noisy quantum processors under aggressive circuit compression?
items.limits: Zero temperature target, open boundary conditions on 36 sites with evolution restricted to 20 Trotter steps (Jt = 12). State preparation fidelity averaged over spin channels is > 0.6.
items.tools: IonQ Forte Enterprise 36-qubit processor · Variational circuit compression · Ancilla-free local kick protocol · Correction-vector DMRG (DMRG-CV) · Error mitigation
items.caption: Longitudinal (S^zz), transverse (S^xx), and total (S_tot) dynamical structure factors plotted as frequency ω/J against momentum q/π across four transverse fields h_x/J ∈0, 0.764, 1.146, 1.604, comparing DMRG-CV, DMRG+Trotter, and error-mitigated hardware measurements.
items.abstract: The collective excitation spectra of quantum magnets provide a direct test of quantum computers as tools for studying strongly correlated matter. Hardware noise limits the circuit depths available for these calculations, leaving the question of how much magnetic information can survive circuit compression. Using IonQ's 36 qubit Forte Enterprise processor, we simulate the magnetic excitation spectra and spin dynamics of a 36 site Heisenberg XXZ chain describing the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 in a transverse field using quantum circuits containing just 420 two qubit gates. The workflow combines an ancilla free local kick protocol with classical tensor network compression, encoding both ground state preparation and time evolution. The reconstructed dynamical structure factors capture the evolution from a broad two spinon continuum toward a dispersive branch with magnon character near the expected critical field. We observe an interesting field driven sign reversal of the nearest neighbor spin correlations which shows a complementary signature of this magnetic evolution. Our error mitigation methods bring the reconstructed total spectra into close agreement with density matrix renormalization group calculations, with Pearson correlation and structural similarity above 0.9 and normalized mean squared error below 0.15. We also perform comparisons with experimental inelastic neutron scattering measurements to connect the recovered excitations to the material's magnetic response. Our results demonstrate that circuit compression and error mitigation allow noisy quantum processors to recover both collective excitations and local magnetic correlations providing a quantitative benchmark for quantum spectroscopy and a basis for extending these methods to more complex magnetic systems.

items.title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation
items.authors: Jielun Chen, Jiace Sun, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Compiling multi-excitonic Bethe-Salpeter equation Hamiltonians into first-quantized block encodings requires widetildeO(N) Toffolis and O(logN) logical qubits, or widetildeO(√N) Toffolis and widetildeO(√N) qubits. Triexciton eigenvalue estimation in ∼10³-atom semiconductors reduces Toffoli counts by 10⁶--10⁷ relative to full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation.
items.question: Can quantum simulation of material excited states be made computationally practical on fault-tolerant hardware by operating within a classical quasiparticle Bethe-Salpeter equation framework rather than simulating the full electronic Hamiltonian?

items.caption: Toffoli and logical qubit counts vs k-point mesh size N_k for diamond triexciton (m=3) eigenvalue estimation at 0.1eV precision, comparing full-Hamiltonian simulation methods with BSE implementations.
items.abstract: The first-principles quantum simulation of the full electronic Hamiltonian of a material model of realistic size appears daunting even in a future era of fully fault-tolerant quantum computers. In contrast, classical simulations of material excited states rely on heuristic quasiparticle frameworks, such as the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation, where only a few quasiparticles are explicitly considered. Here we give a detailed description of quasiparticle quantum simulation for multi-excitonic states within the BSE. We develop an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, and reduce its cost using integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For a materials model of size N, and a fixed number of quasiparticles, the resulting algorithms require widetildeO(N) Toffoli gates and O(logN) logical qubits, or, using space-time tradeoffs, widetildeO(√N) Toffoli gates and widetildeO(√N) logical qubits, achieving up to a sixth power reduction in Toffoli count, or up to exponential reduction in qubit count, versus standard full Hamiltonian simulation techniques that have been explored in materials simulation. Resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation across a range of semiconductor models of a realistic physical size of O(10³) atoms, show that our Toffoli-optimized implementation reduces the Toffoli count by 10⁶-10⁷ relative to full Hamiltonian simulation estimates, while a qubit-optimized implementation requires only a few hundred logical qubits. More broadly, these results show that classical heuristic frameworks will be essential in the design of future fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for materials.

items.title: Ordering-Aware Theory of Trotter Error
items.authors: Zhenning Liu, Zhi-Yuan Wei, Michael Foss-Feig, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Andrew M. Childs
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Constructed efficiently computable, ordering-sensitive finite-step Trotter error bounds for arbitrarily high-order product formulas on geometrically local Hamiltonians. For product formulas of order p > 2, bounds improve on previous analytical bounds by several orders of magnitude and overestimate actual error by only 40%-50%.
items.question: How can term ordering be accounted for to accurately bound Trotter error and efficiently find the optimal gate sequence in product-formula simulations?
items.prior: Commutator-norm bounds overestimated 4th-order Trotter steps by 5–7× (Childs et al. 2021) and single-step errors by 1 order of magnitude at 2nd order and 3 orders at 4th order (Schubert & Mendl 2016).
items.limits: Demonstrated primarily on 1D nearest-neighbor translation-invariant chains. Evaluates error for a specific step size τ rather than providing an analytic τ^(p+1) scaling prefactor.
items.tools: finite-window exact local dynamics · minimum-mean-weight cycle via Karp's algorithm · weighted de Bruijn graph · Suzuki-Trotter product formulas
items.caption: Empirical cumulative distribution of the optimality ratio (actual circuit error divided by minimum error among all 64 ordering patterns) for 4th- and 6th-order product formulas on 500 random 8-qubit chains. Unrestricted Karp optimization selects sequential circuits within 3.5% and 4.2% of optimal on average, while depth-3 Karp optimization selects wave-like circuits that strongly outperform fixed even-odd brickwall circuits.
items.abstract: Product formulas are a basic tool for simulating quantum many-body dynamics, but a fundamental degree of freedom in their application---the ordering of Hamiltonian terms---has remained largely unexplored. Here we systematically study such ordering effects, quantifying their impact on simulation accuracy and exploiting them to design more accurate product-formula simulations. We develop an efficiently computable, ordering-sensitive bound on the finite-step-size Trotter error for geometrically local Hamiltonians for arbitrarily high-order product formulas. For translation-invariant one-dimensional chains, our bounds are close to exact second-, fourth-, and sixth-order Trotter errors in small-system tests, while on large-scale systems they improve on previous higher-order analytical bounds by orders of magnitude. We further use the local structure of the error bounds and estimates to optimize ordering efficiently, reducing the long-chain problem to a minimum-mean-weight-cycle problem on a weighted de Bruijn graph. For random translation-invariant chains, sequential (staircase-like) orderings consistently outperform standard brickwall circuits; when circuit depth is restricted, the optimizer instead favors wave-like parallel-sequential orderings, which preserve much of the accuracy advantage over brickwall circuits. These results establish ordering as a useful degree of freedom for both understanding and improving product-formula simulation.

items.title: A Basis-Aware Approach to Quantum Sampling of the Fermi-Hubbard Ladder
items.authors: Adam Leicester, Zixu Wang, Jack Mandell, Yangyang Xu, Osama Muhammad Raisuddin, Haimeng Zhang, Jian Shi
items.matched: Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator
items.result: Momentum-basis sampling reaches 0.47% relative energy error using 1.4% of the fixed particle-number sector at U/t=1, compared to 9.5% error using 33% of the sector in position basis under identical Krylov constructions.
items.question: To what extent can one-body orbital basis rotations improve the sampling efficiency and ground-state compressibility of sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization on the Fermi-Hubbard ladder?
items.prior: Position-basis sample-based quantum diagonalization (was 9.5% relative error at 33% sector size for U/t=1).
items.limits: At intermediate coupling U/t_leg=5 and isotropic hopping t_rung/t_leg=1, compressibility remains poor, requiring k_(0.99)∝3.106^N/N states to capture 99% ground-state weight; hardware simulations face significant particle-number leakage at large sizes.
items.tools: Sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SKQD) · Density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) · IBM Quantum hardware (ibm_miami up to 120 qubits) · Fulqrum configuration recovery
items.caption: Plots relative energy error |E-E₀|/|E₀| against retained subspace fraction for a 10-site Fermi-Hubbard ladder under position- and momentum-basis sampling across various interaction strengths U/t, Trotter step sizes Δt, and mixing layer counts L.
items.abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization can reduce the classical cost of many-body calculations by restricting diagonalization to configurations identified through quantum sampling, but its efficiency depends on how compactly the target state is represented in the sampled basis. We investigate this dependence for sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization of the half-filled Fermi-Hubbard ladder using physically motivated one-body orbital rotations. Across position, momentum, bonding/antibonding, and leg-mode representations, the most compressible basis varies systematically with interaction strength and hopping anisotropy, with momentum sampling favored in the weakly interacting regime and geometry- or interaction-adapted representations becoming advantageous as the dominant energy scale changes. Near intermediate interaction and isotropic hopping, however, even the most favorable representation remains poorly compressible. Statevector SKQD calculations further show that basis choice strongly affects sampling efficiency. Hardware calculations on systems containing up to 120 qubits retain qualitative signatures of this basis dependence while revealing increasing particle-number leakage and reconstruction sensitivity with system size. These results show that scalable sample-based diagonalization requires co-design of the sampled representation, quantum circuit, and classical reconstruction procedure.

items.title: Two-body control of noiseless subsystems with mixed SU(3) representations lifts teleportation above the classical fidelity limit
items.authors: Otavio A. D. Molitor, Sergii Strelchuk, Michał Studziński
items.matched: Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling
items.result: Adjacent exchanges and one singlet-projector interaction between fundamental and dual qutrits generate all special unitary gates independently across all noiseless subsystems for any r,s≥1. For four-qutrit encoded teleportation under correlated Weyl noise, logical fidelity exceeds the classical bound 1/2 while unencoded teleportation is entanglement breaking.
items.question: Can two-body symmetry-preserving interactions provide independent logical control across a mixed register of fundamental and dual qutrits without extra initialized ancillas?
items.prior: Fundamental-qutrit registers required three-body interactions for semi-universality, or two-body interactions using six ancillas (Hulse et al. 2021).
items.limits: Pure and mixed tensor SU(3) collective noise only; gate sequence synthesis algorithm not provided; requires retaining trials where all 4 (or 5) qutrits arrive; diamond-norm perturbation bounds assume input-independent survival probabilities.
items.tools: walled Brauer algebra · Lie-algebra control theory · mixed Schur-Weyl duality · correlated Weyl noise channel model · numerical pulse sequence optimization
items.caption: Teleportation fidelity plotted against transmission noise parameter. Identifies the noise interval where unencoded teleportation drops below the entanglement-breaking threshold while encoded teleportation stays above the classical fidelity bound of 1/2.
items.abstract: Collective noise can leave degrees of freedom unaffected, allowing them to store quantum information. Processing this information also requires physically available logical gates. We consider r fundamental qutrits transforming under U∈SU(3) and s dual qutrits transforming under its complex conjugate overlineU, with collective action R_(r,s)(U)=U^(⊗r)⊗overlineU^(⊗s). Using the image of the walled Brauer algebra and Lie-algebra arguments, we show that adjacent exchanges within each qutrit type and one singlet-projector interaction between the two types generate any independently chosen family of special unitary gates on the noiseless subsystems by a finite pulse sequence, for every r,s≥1. This establishes semi-universality of this system. We illustrate the result with a numerically optimised sequence of 24 pulses for three fundamental qutrits and one dual qutrit. We then use the encoding and available logical corrections for qutrit teleportation under correlated Weyl noise. Under explicit assumptions on channel composition and which trials are retained, and allowing for baseline implementation errors, we identify noise ranges in which encoded teleportation exceeds the classical fidelity bound of 1/2, while the unencoded teleportation channel is entanglement breaking. We analyse fidelity on accepted trials separately from the transmission costs of the additional physical qutrits.

items.title: Rate-Optimal Quantum Discrete Simulation Optimization
items.authors: Mingjie Hu, Jian-Qiang Hu
items.matched: Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation
items.result: Quantum discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap Ω(|X|/T), achieved up to logarithmic factors by the textscQUEST algorithm (O(|X|logT/T)). Convergence rate improves quadratically over budget T compared to classical bound Ω(√|X|/T), with worse scaling in decision count |X|.
items.question: How does quantum computing affect the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting, and can a provably rate-optimal algorithm be designed?
items.prior: Classical discrete simulation optimization has minimax expected optimality gap lower bound Ω(√|X|/T).
items.limits: Fixed-budget setting with discrete candidate decisions |X|. Continuous observation outputs require finite support discretization onto grid qubits.
items.tools: sequential quantum phase-testing lower bound reduction · quantum Monte Carlo estimation · sequential elimination framework · slow-measurement mechanism · Qiskit numerical simulation
items.caption: Expected optimality gap as a function of simulation budget T under Bernoulli outcomes with |X|=20. Compares the faster decay of the quantum textscQUEST algorithm against the classical textscMC-EST baseline.
items.abstract: Quantum computing has developed rapidly in recent years and has shown potential advantages over classical computing in various domains. In this paper, we study whether quantum computing can accelerate the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization in the fixed-budget setting. We first formulate the quantum discrete simulation optimization problem by defining the quantum simulation oracle, the algorithmic performance measure, and the corresponding optimality guarantee. Based on this formulation, we establish a minimax lower bound on the expected optimality gap for any quantum algorithm. The lower bound analysis reduces the discrete simulation optimization problem to a sequential quantum phase-testing problem, and the resulting lower-bound argument may be of independent interest. By comparing the quantum lower bound with its classical counterpart, we show that the optimal convergence rate in the quantum setting exhibits a quadratic improvement in its dependence on the simulation budget, at the cost of a worse dependence on the number of decisions. We then propose the first fixed-budget quantum algorithm, called textscQUEST, for discrete simulation optimization. The algorithm combines a quantum Monte Carlo subroutine with a sequential elimination framework and uses a slow-measurement mechanism to help preserve quantum superposition during the optimization process. We prove that textscQUEST achieves the optimal convergence rate up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments further show that textscQUEST outperforms its classical counterpart, which provides empirical evidence for the quantum advantage in improving the convergence rate of discrete simulation optimization algorithms.

items.title: Quantum Key Distribution with Entanglement-Swapped Photons from a Quantum Emitter
items.authors: Michele B. Rota, Francesco Basso Basset, Alessandro Laneve, Francesco Salusti, Nicolas Claro-Rodriguez, Giuseppe Ronco, Mattia Beccaceci, Tobias M. Krieger, Quirin Buchinger, Saimon F. Covre da Silva, Sandra Stroj, Mariia Gumberidze, Vladyslav Usenko, Sven Höfling, Tobias Huber-Loyola, Mario A. Usuga Castaneda, Armando Rastelli, Klaus D. Jöns, Rinaldo Trotta
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Secret key distribution implemented using entanglement-swapped photons from a GaAs quantum dot, yielding an estimated secure key rate of 1×10⁻³bit at optimal 30ps BSM temporal post-selection.
items.question: Can correlated photons generated from a deterministic quantum emitter and distributed via all-photonic entanglement swapping support secure quantum key distribution?
items.limits: Asymptotic limit. Employs single-emitter temporal multiplexing rather than independent remote quantum dots; requires high temporal filtering (30ps) to overcome distinguishability limits.
items.tools: strain-tuned GaAs/AlGaAs quantum dot in circular Bragg resonator · resonant two-photon excitation (biexciton-exciton cascade) · linear optics Bell state measurement (BSM) · asymmetric source-independent Ekert QKD protocol · high-resolution temporal post-selection
items.caption: Quantum bit error rate (QBER) and Bell parameter S plotted against BSM coincidence time window. Shows the trade-off where narrower time windows reduce error and push S above the classical limit of 2.
items.abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a fundamental functionality of quantum networks. Extending its range requires quantum repeaters, a technology still under development and not yet demonstrated in combination with quantum cryptographic protocols. Here, we address the elementary operation of a viable quantum repeater scheme by evaluating whether correlated photons distributed via entanglement swapping can support secret key distribution. We employ a state-of-the-art deterministic photon source based on a strain-tuned GaAs quantum dot embedded in a photonic cavity and implement a source-independent QKD protocol between two nodes using entanglement-swapped photons. We benchmark the system and present how high-resolution temporal post-selection can enable secure key exchange, with further rate improvements expected through realistic device and protocol optimizations. Due to its compatibility with a wide range of quantum memory platforms, our approach represents a significant step towards long-distance quantum-safe communication.

items.title: The QICK Box: A Modular RF Front-End System for Quantum Control and Readout
items.authors: L. Arnaldi, D. Martin, S. Sussman, S. Uemura, K. Treptow, N. Wilcer, A. Colón Cesaní, O. Seidel, K. Anyang, G. Bratrud, F. Abouzahr, J. Christiansen-Salameh, D. Baxter, G. Cancelo
items.matched: Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play
items.result: Modular companion front-end for AMD ZCU216 RFSoC provides up to 16 outputs, 8 inputs, and 8 20-bit DC biases, achieving (91.7±0.4)% single-shot readout fidelity and SNR of 4.4±0.1 without a quantum amplifier.
items.question: Can an integrated, modular RF/DC companion board for the ZCU216 eliminate external room-temperature signal conditioning while maintaining high-fidelity qubit readout?
items.limits: Readout fidelity limited by T₁ = 58.3±4.1 μs relaxation during the 5.6 μs readout pulse (causing (4.7±0.3)% error); residual ≈3.6% error from 44mK effective qubit thermal population and state overlap.
items.tools: AMD ZCU216 Gen3 RFSoC FPGA · Modular RF and DC input/output daughtercards · ADMV8818 programmable bandpass filters · PE43705 digital step attenuators · Six-transmon superconducting device
items.caption: Rotated I-Q scatter plot and projected histograms for 3000 single shots per state (|g⟩ and |e⟩), showing distinct clusters separated by Δμ= 28±0.2a.u. with clean-side noise width barσ=6.5±0.1a.u.
items.abstract: The QICK (Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit), first introduced in 2022, is a standalone open source control system for quantum information science. Since then, QICK has been migrated to new hardware platforms, expanded its functionality for applications with different types of qubits (superconducting, atomic, ion-trapped, and spin defects), as well as quantum sensors, and quantum networks. QICK is a highly optimized control kit, with a library of functions that can be used for more than one application. In particular, the software and firmware are customized to minimize latency and maximize control performance and throughput. In this white paper, we describe hardware details and performance of the QICK Box. The QICK Box features up to 16 outputs, up to 8 inputs, and 8 20-bit DC biases. Modular output and input daughtercards give the choice of signal chains optimized for fast DC-coupled signals or RF signals up to 10 GHz. Power levels, step attenuation, and bandpass filtering are controlled by software. We demonstrate the system's performance through single-shot readout measurements of a six-transmon device at the Quantum Underground Instrumentation Experimental Testbed (QUIET) at Fermilab, achieving (91.7 +/- 0.4)% readout fidelity limited by T1 decay during the readout. The single shot readout signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is 4.4 +/- 0.1 without a quantum amplifier, confirming that the QICK Box is suitable for high-fidelity quantum control and measurement applications. Advances in firmware and software will be described in a separate paper.

items.title: Beyond Pure Dephasing: Quantum Error Correction in Single Molecules Requires Multiple Spins
items.authors: Matteo Mezzadri, Silvia Macedonio, Luca Lepori, Emilio Macaluso, Francesco Albarelli, Richard E. P. Winpenny, Alessandro Chiesa, Stefano Carretta1
items.matched: transmon and fluxonium coherence, single- and two-qubit gate fidelity
items.result: Two-level error-correcting encoding combines embedded dephasing correction in S-mathscrs molecular spin dimers with an outer multi-qubit code, bypassing the loss of transferred coherence in anharmonic qudits.
items.question: How can fault-tolerant quantum error correction handle both diagonal dephasing and off-diagonal relaxation errors in single-molecule spin architectures?
items.limits: Simulated under Markovian secular spin-bath dynamics at B_z=0.35 T; assumes ideal syndrome measurement and two-qubit gates on the outer code; inter-molecule entanglement mechanisms not implemented.
items.tools: Redfield master equation · Knill–Laflamme conditions · Pauli twirling approximation · Steane [[7,1,3]] code · Star-shaped multi-spin clusters
items.caption: Entanglement infidelity P_err of planar logical rotations versus dephasing time T₂ for embedded S=3/2 and S=7/2 units at different relaxation times T₁, compared against bare spin-1/2 qubits.
items.abstract: We propose multi-spin molecules as a viable architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing. To this aim, we introduce a correction protocol handling both diagonal and off-diagonal errors, typically associated with dephasing and relaxation. The scheme is based on a hybrid encoding which combines dephasing-tolerant units suppressing the leading pure dephasing error into a multi-spin molecule implementing a multi-qubit code for residual off-diagonal errors. Our proposal leverages peculiar properties of molecular spins, i.e. the strong hierarchy between different errors and the possibility to engineer multi-spin molecules at the synthetic level. Moreover, it addresses the important issue of the loss of coherences in anharmonic systems subject to off-diagonal errors, which hampers their correction at the single spin level. Thanks to the huge suppression of dephasing by the first-level code, we numerically demonstrate the potential performance of this strategy even with a limited number of spins per logical unit.

items.title: Extracting the anyon charge from shot noise in complex fractional quantum Hall edges
items.authors: Jinhong Park, Christian Spranslätt
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Heating corrections to the QPC Fano factor scale as O(T^(-1/2)) for auto-correlation and O(T^(1/2)) for cross-correlation, while a combined clean Fano factor F_clean eliminates outer-arm heating to achieve O(T^(3/2)) scaling and extract the anyon charge e^*/e=1/3.
items.question: How can the intrinsic quasiparticle charge be extracted from shot noise in multichannel fractional quantum Hall edges where intermode equilibration and heating obscure quantum point contact partition noise?
items.limits: Analyzed for the ν=2/3 fractional quantum Hall state in the strong charge-equilibration regime (ℓ_ch≪L) and weak-transmission limit (T≪1).
items.tools: discrete network line-junction model · continuum charge and thermal transport equations · four-terminal QPC scattering framework
items.caption: Excess current noises ΔS_auto, -ΔS_cross, and resulting Fano factors plotted against dimensionless bias e^*V₀/(k_BT₀). Shows F_clean staying close to e^*/e=1/3 while F_auto diverges and F_cross underestimates the charge.
items.abstract: Shot-noise measurements with a quantum point contact provide a direct probe of the quasiparticle charge in Laughlin fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states. However, the interpretation of such measurements becomes more subtle for multichannel edges, where the point-contact tunneling noise coexists with noise generated by intermode equilibration and heating. We develop a general framework that incorporates both these contributions and apply it to the paradigmatic ν=2/3 FQH edge. We derive expressions for the drain auto- and cross-correlations in a four-terminal QPC geometry and show that equilibration-induced heating affects the auto- and cross-correlations in parametrically different way than the intrinsic partition noise. This distinction permits us to propose a specific combination of the two correlations which strongly suppresses the heating contribution and fully recovers the tunneling quasiparticle charge. Our results thereby provide a systematic framework for interpreting shot-noise measurements in complex FQH edges and can be further extended to more general counterpropagating edge structures.

items.title: Design Automation for Gray-Code Quantum Read-Only Memory
items.authors: Hao-Yu Lu, Yu-Ting Kao, Yeong-Jar Chang, Chao-Hung Wang, Darsen D. Lu
items.matched: Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play
items.result: Gray code quantum read-only memory (GQROM) and an automated EDA flow reduce state transition complexity and gate-induced errors for loading classical data into quantum circuits.
items.question: How to design a scalable, low-overhead programmable quantum read-only memory to load classical data into quantum circuits?
items.limits: Simulated and validated on Qiskit framework.
items.tools: Gray code encoding · Qiskit platform · electronic design automation (EDA) flow
items.abstract: We propose a programmable quantum read-only memory based on Gray code encoding, termed GQROM, designed to efficiently load classical data into quantum circuits. This architecture mitigates critical bottlenecks in near-term quantum computing by reducing initialization overhead and gate-induced errors. By utilizing Gray code, in which consecutive addresses differ by only a single bit, GQROM minimizes state transition complexity. We demonstrate the architecture's flexibility in accessing targeted data through initial-state modification. The entire design, including a systematic EDA flow, was implemented and validated on the Qiskit platform, confirming its practical feasibility. These results underscore GQROM's potential as a scalable and hardware-friendly solution for efficient state preparation in quantum circuits.

items.title: Gap-Protected Heisenberg-Limited Squeezing with Locally Interacting Multi-Level Spins
items.authors: Sakshi Bahamnia, Sagar Chaudhary, Arman Duha, Thomas Bilitewski
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Adding local su(D) exchange interactions restores Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing ξ² ∝1/N in multi-level spin arrays across spatial dimensions d=1,2,3 for any power-law interaction exponent α.
items.question: Can gap protection enable Heisenberg-limited spin squeezing in multi-level qudit arrays with finite-range interactions?
items.prior: Without protection, squeezing scales as ξ²_min ∝N^(-ν) with ν≈1 only for αlesssimd/2, degrading to ν≈1/2 at α=d and νlesssim0.05 for αgtrsim3d/2.
items.limits: Valid during early-time exponential growth regime before depletion (n_(i,±1) ≪1). Assumes periodic boundary conditions and gap-protection strength above critical threshold χgtrsimχ_c(L).
items.tools: Bogoliubov spin-wave theory · Discrete truncated Wigner approximation (dTWA) · SU(3) Casimir gap protection · Schwinger boson mapping
items.caption: Minimal spin squeezing parameter ξ²_min and scaling exponent ν versus gap protection strength χ, showing the transition to Heisenberg scaling ξ²_min ∝1/N in 1D, 2D, and 3D arrays.
items.abstract: We demonstrate a general mechanism to generate scalable, metrologically useful entanglement in the form of generalized spin squeezing in multi-level (qudit) spin systems with power-law interactions. We demonstrate this for spin-changing dynamics, extending the physics of spin-nematic squeezing known from spinor BECs to spatially extended lattice geometries. In the absence of all-to-all connectivity, the dynamics generally suffers from leakage into non-collective finite-momentum modes, destroying Heisenberg scaling. We show that introducing local su(D) exchange interactions establishes an energy gap that protects the fully symmetric collective manifold, suppressing non-collective excitations, and achieving Heisenberg scaling ξ²∝1/N in one to three dimensions for any power-law exponent. We provide an analytical understanding of the mechanism via the analysis of the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, and demonstrate its effectiveness via numerical simulations of the quantum many-body dynamics. Our findings more broadly apply to other spin-squeezing Hamiltonians, and directly generalize to larger internal spin dimensions. Our results provide a practical pathway towards scalable Heisenberg-limited qudit entanglement generation in experimental platforms such as arrays of (polar) molecules, magnetic atoms, and Rydberg atoms realizing multi-level spin systems.

items.title: Chiral Vacuum Engineering of Quantum Hall Matter
items.authors: Kiran M. Kulkarni, Andrey Baydin, Motoaki Bamba, Junichiro Kono, Ceren B. Dag, Vasil Rokaj
items.matched: Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…
items.result: Coupling a 2DEG to a chiral cavity isolates resonant from antiresonant vacuum interactions, yielding a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity ρ_xy^((s)) = h/(νe²) - s m^*γ² D / (n_2D e² ω_cav²) and an unsqueezed or two-mode squeezed ground state for co- or counter-rotating modes.
items.question: How does a circularly polarized, time-reversal-symmetry-breaking chiral cavity vacuum modify the polariton spectrum, ground state, and DC magnetotransport of a two-dimensional electron gas?
items.prior: In achiral or linearly polarized cavities, Hall resistivity is immune to polariton broadening and light-matter coupling at zero temperature, satisfying ρ_xy^ach = h/(νe²).
items.limits: Spatially uniform cavity field (Kohn's theorem center-of-mass coupling), leading order in polariton broadening γ, zero temperature.
items.tools: Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian · Hopfield-Bogoliubov diagonalization · SU(2) and SU(1,1) algebraic symmetries · Drude-type DC transport inversion
items.caption: Polariton eigenspectra, longitudinal resistivity, and Hall resistivity versus magnetic field B for counter-rotating (CRI) and co-rotating (CRA) chiral cavity modes, showing mode crossing versus anticrossing and handedness-dependent Hall corrections.
items.abstract: We reveal that a chiral cavity distinguishes the resonant and antiresonant interactions between a two-dimensional electron gas and the cavity vacuum. For co-rotating helicities, the modes anticross, exhibiting vacuum Rabi splitting, and retain a bare vacuum ground state. For counter-rotating helicities, the modes cross, acquiring vacuum-mediated energy shifts and a two-mode squeezed ground state. We trace the origin of these observations to the SU(2) and SU(1,1) symmetries of the respective Hamiltonians and present their spectroscopic signatures in chiral photonic crystal cavities. We further predict that cavity chirality produces a handedness-dependent correction to Hall resistivity at finite polariton broadening, while such a correction is not present in an achiral cavity. For the longitudinal resistivity, we find an asymmetric response of the Shubnikov--de Haas oscillations for the different helicities. Finally, we present an experimentally accessible route for detecting the squeezed ground state through current fluctuations. Parameters based on a recently demonstrated terahertz chiral cavity place these effects within experimental reach.

items.title: Quasiparticle quantum simulation of materials with the Bethe-Salpeter equation
items.authors: Jielun Chen, Jiace Sun, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan
items.matched: Semiconductor spin qubits
items.result: Compiling multi-excitonic Bethe-Salpeter equation Hamiltonians into first-quantized block encodings requires widetildeO(N) Toffolis and O(logN) logical qubits, or widetildeO(√N) Toffolis and widetildeO(√N) qubits. Triexciton eigenvalue estimation in ∼10³-atom semiconductors reduces Toffoli counts by 10⁶--10⁷ relative to full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation.
items.question: Can quantum simulation of material excited states be made computationally practical on fault-tolerant hardware by operating within a classical quasiparticle Bethe-Salpeter equation framework rather than simulating the full electronic Hamiltonian?
items.prior: Full-Hamiltonian quantum simulation of a 10×10×10 diamond mesh required 3.7×10¹⁷ Toffolis in second quantization (THC) and 4.2×10¹⁸ Toffolis in first quantization (plane waves).
items.limits: Heuristic GW/Bethe-Salpeter equation framework with static screened interaction and Tamm-Dancoff approximation; fixed quasiparticle count m_tot=2m.
items.tools: First-quantized orbital-based block encoding · Tensor hypercontraction (THC) integral factorization · Qubitization · Space-group symmetry adaptation
items.caption: Toffoli and logical qubit counts vs k-point mesh size N_k for diamond triexciton (m=3) eigenvalue estimation at 0.1eV precision, comparing full-Hamiltonian simulation methods with BSE implementations.
items.abstract: The first-principles quantum simulation of the full electronic Hamiltonian of a material model of realistic size appears daunting even in a future era of fully fault-tolerant quantum computers. In contrast, classical simulations of material excited states rely on heuristic quasiparticle frameworks, such as the GW approximation and Bethe-Salpeter equation, where only a few quasiparticles are explicitly considered. Here we give a detailed description of quasiparticle quantum simulation for multi-excitonic states within the BSE. We develop an explicit first-quantized, orbital-based block encoding of the multi-exciton BSE Hamiltonian for qubitization, and reduce its cost using integral factorization and crystal symmetries. For a materials model of size N, and a fixed number of quasiparticles, the resulting algorithms require widetildeO(N) Toffoli gates and O(logN) logical qubits, or, using space-time tradeoffs, widetildeO(√N) Toffoli gates and widetildeO(√N) logical qubits, achieving up to a sixth power reduction in Toffoli count, or up to exponential reduction in qubit count, versus standard full Hamiltonian simulation techniques that have been explored in materials simulation. Resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of triexcitonic eigenvalue estimation across a range of semiconductor models of a realistic physical size of O(10³) atoms, show that our Toffoli-optimized implementation reduces the Toffoli count by 10⁶-10⁷ relative to full Hamiltonian simulation estimates, while a qubit-optimized implementation requires only a few hundred logical qubits. More broadly, these results show that classical heuristic frameworks will be essential in the design of future fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for materials.
